utterances.text: Thank you. And now the Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. I'm Toma Fila, and together with Vladimir Petrovic I represent the Defence of Nikola Sainovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with my co-counsel, Aleksander Aleksic, and legal assistant, Cathy MacDaid, and we represent General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of General Lazarevic, Mihajlo Bakrac and Djuro Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Dragan Ivetic for Mr. Sreten Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, counsels. The Prosecution and the Defence have lodged appeals against the judgement rendered on the 26th February 2009 by Trial Chamber III of the Tribunal. According to the order issued on the 18th January 2013 and the 31st January 2013, the Appeals Chamber will presently hear the appeals in this case. This case concerns the criminal responsibility for Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Pavkovic, Mr. Lazarevic, and Mr. Lukic for the forcible displacement of the Albanian population in Kosovo between March and June 1999. The defendants were charged with deportation, other inhumane acts, forcible transfer, murder and the persecution through murder, sexual assault, and the destruction of cultural property as crimes against humanity and murder as a violation of laws or customs of war under Article 7(1) and Article 7(3) of the Tribunal's Statute. The Trial Chamber found that during the indictment period a joint criminal enterprise existed. The common purpose of it was to ensure the continued control by the former Republic of Yugoslavia and the Serbian authorities over Kosovo, and that this was to be achieved by criminal means. The Trial Chamber determined that through a widespread and systematic campaign of terror and violence, the Kosovo Albanian population was to be forcibly displaced, both within and without Kosovo. The Trial Chamber further concluded that while the crimes of deportation and forcible transfer were within the ambit of the common purpose, the crimes of murder, persecution through murder, sexual assault, and the destruction of cultural property fell outside the common purpose. The Trial Chamber found that Mr. Sainovic, the former prime minister of Serbia and deputy prime minister of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, possessed the intent to forcibly displace the Kosovo Albanian population and contributed significantly to the joint criminal enterprise. As the members of the joint criminal enterprise used VJ and MUP forces in furtherance of their common purpose, the crimes committed by these forces in the course of implementing the common purpose were found to be imputable to Mr. Sainovic. With regard to crimes falling outside the common purpose, the Trial Chamber held that the murder of the Kosovo Albanians and the damage and the destruction of the religious property were reasonably foreseeable to Mr. Sainovic while the occurrence of sexual assault was not. The Trial Chamber accordingly found Mr. Sainovic guilty of deportation, other inhumane acts, forcible transfer, murder, and the persecution as crimes against humanity and murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war through his participation in the joint criminal enterprise. Mr. Sainovic was sentenced to a single term of 22 years of imprisonment. Mr. Sainovic presents seven grounds of appeal which focus on four main challenges to the trial judgement. First, he contends that the Trial Chamber violated his right to a fair trial by convicting him on the basis of material facts that were not pleaded in the indictment. Second, he insists that the Trial Chamber erred in its evaluation of the evidence. Third, he challenges the Trial Chamber's conclusion regarding the existence of the joint criminal enterprise in general and his participation therein. Finally, he challenged the sentence imposed by the Trial Chamber. Turning to Mr. Pavkovic, Mr. Pavkovic served as a VJ commander of the 3rd Army from the 13th January 1999 until early 2000 when he became chief of the VJ General Staff. The Trial Chamber found that he shared the intent to forcibly displace the Kosovo Albanian population and that he contributed significantly to the joint criminal enterprise. As the the members of the joint criminal enterprise used VJ and MUP forces in furtherance of their common purpose, the crimes committed by these forces in the course of implementing the common purpose were found to be imputable to Mr. Pavkovic. The Trial Chamber further found that the crimes falling outside the common purpose, namely, murder of the Kosovo Albanians, sexual assault, and the damage and the destruction to religious property were reasonably foreseeable to Mr. Pavkovic. The Trial Chamber accordingly convicted Mr. Pavkovic for deportation, other inhumane acts, forcible transfer, murder, and the persecution as crimes against humanity and murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war. Mr. Pavkovic was sentenced to a single term of 22 years of imprisonment. Mr. Pavkovic sets out 12 grounds of appeal challenging the Trial Chamber on five main points. First, he claims that Trial Chamber violated his right to a fair trial. Second, he asserts that the Trial Chamber erred in its evaluation of the evidence. Third, Mr. Pavkovic challenges the Trial Chamber's finding concerning his individual criminal responsibility. Fourth, he submits that the Trial Chamber erred in law in relation to the chapeau mens rea requirement of crimes against humanity. Finally, he argues that the Trial Chamber erred in its evaluation of the factors relevant to his sentence. Turning to Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Lazarevic was appointed VJ commander of the Pristina Corps on 25th December 1998 and held this position until 28th December 1999, when he was appointed Chief of Staff of the 3rd Army. The Trial Chamber held Mr. Lazarevic responsible for aiding and abetting instances of deportation and forcible transfer, wherein the VJ was involved. Accordingly, the Trial Chamber convicted Mr. Lazarevic of aiding and abetting deportation and other inhumane acts, forcible transfer, and sentenced him to a single term of 15 years of imprisonment. Mr. Lazarevic advances four grounds of appeal. First, he challenges the Trial Chamber's finding concerning certain underlying crimes. Second, he submits that the Trial Chamber erred in its evaluation of the evidence. Third, he claims that the Trial Chamber erred in law and fact when assessing his responsibility for aiding and abetting forcible transfer and deportation. Finally, he asserts that the Trial Chamber failed to assess the relevant circumstances and imposed a sentence that was inappropriately severe. Turning to Mr. Lukic, Mr. Lukic was head of the MUP staff in Pristina from middle 1998, and upon the completion of his assignment in Kosovo he was appointed head of the border police administration of the Serbian Ministry of Interior. The Trial Chamber found Mr. Lukic shared the intent to forcibly displace the Kosovo Albanian population and that he made a significant contribution to the joint criminal enterprise. As the members of the joint criminal enterprise used VJ and MUP forces in furtherance of their common purpose, the crimes committed by these forces in the course of implementing the common purpose were found to be imputable to Mr. Lukic. With regard to the crimes falling outside the common purpose, the Trial Chamber held that the murder of Kosovo Albanians and the damage and the destruction of the religious property were reasonably foreseeable to Mr. Lukic, whereas the occurrence of sexual assaults was not. The Trial Chamber accordingly found Mr. Lukic guilty of deportation, other inhumane acts, forcible transfer, murder, and persecution as crimes against humanity and murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war. Mr. Lukic was sentenced to a single term of 22 years of imprisonment. Mr. Lukic sets out 37 grounds of appeal, challenging the trial judgement on four main points. First, he asserts that the Trial Chamber violated his right to a fair trial on various occasions. Second, he challenges a number of findings concerning underlying crimes committed in various municipalities. Third, he contends that the Trial Chamber erred in assessing the existence of a joint criminal enterprise and his participation therein. Finally, he claims that the Trial Chamber erred in imposing an excessive and disproportionate sentence. The Prosecution presents six grounds of appeal against the trial judgement. First, it requests that the Appeals Chamber convict Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Pavkovic, Mr. Lazarevic, and Mr. Lukic for persecution as a crime against humanity through forcible transfer and the deportations. Second, it requests that the Appeals Chamber convict Mr. Lazarevic for aiding and abetting murder and persecution as a crime against humanity and murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war for the killing at Korenica, Meja and Dubrava. Third, the Prosecution submits that Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Lukic should be convicted for persecution as a crime against humanity for the proven instances of sexual assaults in Beleg and Cirez. Fourth, the Prosecution requests that the Appeals Chamber convict Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Pavkovic, and Mr. Lukic for persecution as a crime against humanity for the additional instances of sexual assaults in Pristina. Fifth, the Prosecution requests that the Appeals Chamber convict Mr. Lazarevic for aiding and abetting deportation and other inhumane acts, forcible transfer, as crimes against humanity with respect to certain locations. The Prosecution submits that the sentences should be increased in the event that these convictions were entered. In any event, the Prosecution submits that the sentences imposed by the Trial Chamber were too low and should be increased. Throughout this hearing, counsel may argue the grounds of appeal in any order it considers suitable for their presentations; however, I would urge counsel not to repeat verbatim or to summarise extensively the arguments presented in their briefs. The Appeals Chamber is familiar with the briefs. Furthermore, the parties are obliged to provide the precise reference to materials supporting their oral arguments. The appeal process is not a trial de novo and the parties should refrain from repeating their case as presented at trial. Arguments must be limited to the alleged error of law which invalidate the trial judgement or alleged error of fact which occasion a miscarriage of justice. In addition to the questions raised by the Appeals Chamber in the order issued on the 20th February 2013, Judges may ask a question at any time in the course of parties' submissions or at the end of the hearings. In view of the jurisprudential development in the recent Perisic appeal judgement, counsel for Mr. Lazarevic and the Prosecution are also invited to advance submissions on aiding and abetting liability in the course of their submissions on Wednesday, 13 March. As set out in the Scheduling Order of 31st January 2013, this hearing will proceed as follows: First, we hear the submissions from the counsel for Mr. Sainovic for one hour. We will then pause for 15 minutes. After counsel for Mr. Sainovic completes his second hour of submissions, the Prosecution will respond for one hour. Following a pause of one hour and 30 minutes, the Prosecution will complete its second hour of response, after which counsel for Mr. Sainovic will reply to Prosecution's response. Tomorrow, we will hear the submissions regarding Mr. Pavkovic's appeal. Counsel for Mr. Lazarevic and Mr. Lukic will present their submissions on Wednesday and Thursday respectively. Finally, on Friday we will hear submissions concerning the Prosecution's appeal. By the end of the hearing, the Defence will each have the opportunity to make a personal address for ten minutes, if they wish to do so. Having now stated the manner in which we will proceed, I would like to invite counsel for Mr. Sainovic to present his appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, Mr. President. Your Honours. In its appeal brief our Defence has stated in detail and precisely all the reasons why it believes that the trial judgement is legally and factually untenable and that this Appeals Chamber should vary that judgement in all the parts establishing the individual criminal responsibility of Mr. Sainovic and return a judgement of acquittal. The Defence stands by fully by its pleadings from the appeals brief. The Defence does not abandon a single one of its grounds or subgrounds of appeal, finding that even after four years from the trial judgement the grounds of appeal are profoundly justified; that the trial judgement is full of contradictions, inclarities, a lack of logic, and legally controversial findings. The Defence believes that this appeal hearing is not an opportunity to repeat all the arguments. The Defence is convinced that this Appeals Chamber has carefully read the submissions of the parties; and therefore, the Defence shall focus its submissions to just a few issues that it believes are of particular importance and sufficiently illustrative to point to the erroneous logic and erroneous conclusions about facts and law which made the Trial Chamber make conclusions that not a single reasonable trier of fact would have made. The Defence will deal here with the finding that Sainovic was a political co-ordinator; the findings related to the existence of the joint criminal enterprise, the so-called Joint Command; the findings related to the events of 1998 that are copied on to year 1999; findings regarding the intent of Mr. Sainovic with regard to the act for which he was convicted by the trial judgement; and the sentence. Joint criminal enterprise para 61, 62, and 64. The Defence will first deal with the issue of existence of the joint criminal enterprise, whose purpose, according to the trial judgement, was to ensure the continued control of FRY and Serbia over Kosovo through the commission of crimes, widespread and systematic campaign of terror and violence which resulted in the forced displacement of the Albanian population of Kosovo inside and outside of Kosovo, 95, Volume III. The Trial Chamber has no first-hand evidence of a criminal plan and therefore seeks and finds evidence of its existence in the pattern of events, 17, Volume III. What does the Trial Chamber do in its attempt to establish the existence of a criminal plan? There is no direct evidence of existence of a plan; however, there are a plethora of witnesses who clearly testified there was no plan. They never heard of one; they never saw one. These are witnesses who, in view of their position and work they carried out in 1999, must have known if a plan had existed. However, the Trial Chamber rejects the testimony of all these witnesses, direct participants in the events, and says that these witnesses who claim there was no plan either had a motive to lie to protect themselves and others or were simply not in a position to know of a plan or are simply speculating based on inadequate information, 93, Volume III. The Trial Chamber does not even explain why it believes that these witnesses are not telling the truth. It simply says that the witnesses who say there was no plan are lying. However, not even the witnesses that are not called liars by the Trial Chamber also know nothing about a plan. Numerous foreigners in Kosovo who monitored the Serb side in numerous documents and their evidence before the Trial Chamber also failed to provide a shred of evidence about a plan. These witnesses include people who headed large teams made up as a rule of military officers from NATO member countries, OSCE mission, the Contact Group, diplomatic observer missions, et cetera. These witnesses, too, know nothing of a plan, but the Trial Chamber does not say they were lying. The Trial Chamber found that a plan existed and that the accused were waiting for the attack of the most powerful military alliance in the world in order to realise their criminal plan under those circumstances. The Chamber, therefore, concludes that out of all the possible situations, Serbia and the FRY were waiting for the least favourable one, the conflict of Serbia with NATO, the only one of all situations that could certainly not end in FRY and Serbia's victory. The allegation that the air strikes, that is to say war with NATO, was the opportunity they were waiting for to displace Kosovo civilians, 90, Volume III, is a finding that not a single reasonable trier of fact would have made. Therefore, the Serbs were waiting to be attacked by NATO to start implementing their permanent goal: Kosovo without Albanians, which was contrary to the NATO objective in that war. Serbs, therefore, according to the finding of the Trial Chamber, moved to implement a plan that was possible to implement only if they defeat NATO. The Trial Chamber notes that at least 700.000 Kosovo Albanians left Kosovo as a result of deliberate actions of the FRY and Serbia's forces, 1178, Volume II. The Chamber, however, rules out all the other reasons why the population was leaving their homes. The Trial Chamber fails to consider the consequences of the bombing of the civilian convoy with Kosovo Albanians near Djakovica in April 1999 or the bombing of Korisa village in May 1999 or the bus near Luzine village in May 1999. And how many people out of the minimum 700.000 left out of fear from these mass deaths caused by NATO bombing? The NATO was bombing towns, Pec, Djakovica. What is happening with their population? We have evidence of that in the case including very credible evidence obtained under Rule 70, but the Trial Chamber ignores and neglects everything that does not fit the previously defined picture. In its appeals brief the Defence, as part of its sixth ground of appeal, provided other reasons why it finds the conclusion of the existence of the criminal plan unfounded. Nikola Sainovic was designated in the indictment pleaded by the Prosecutor before the Trial Chamber also as the commander of the Joint Command which commanded, controlled, guided, and otherwise exerted effective control over FRY and Serbia's forces in Kosovo. Nikola Sainovic put up a defence against these charges. And this Defence team concludes that his defence was successful because the trial judgement does not state anywhere that Sainovic was the commander of the Joint Command, nor that he commanded or controlled VJ and MUP of Serbia forces in Kosovo at the indicted time. However, instead of acquitting Sainovic from the charges of the Prosecution that Sainovic was the commander of the Joint Command is not proven, the Trial Chamber convicts him to years of imprisonment for something that he was never charged with. The Trial Chamber convicted Sainovic as the political co-ordinator of VJ and MUP forces in Kosovo. Sainovic -- Sainovic's Defence was not against his political co-ordination of forces in Kosovo. His defence was against charges that he commanded these forces, that he planned and ordered their use. If Sainovic had been informed that he was not charged as the commander of the Joint Command but as a political co-ordinator, his defence case would have been probably conceived in a different way. He would have brought different witnesses and led evidence of different facts. The Defence wishes to emphasise that by virtue of the fact that Sainovic was not charged as political co-ordinator but as the commander of the Joint Command commanding VJ and MUP forces, Sainovic was denied the right to a fair trial. Of course, in the eyes of the Defence what is controversial is not only the fact that Sainovic was convicted for something he was not charged with. Deeply controversial in the opinion of this Defence is the very content of the conclusions on Sainovic as a political co-ordination. In paragraph 331, Volume III, the Trial Chamber states that the VJ and the MUP associated themselves with politicians, that the VJ and MUP had to seek approval from Milosevic, and that is why Sainovic's role was decisive. The Trial Chamber uses three groups of evidence to attempt to prove this allegation: A, meetings designated as meetings of the Joint Command; B, other meetings; and C, a string of claims that Sainovic -- that attempt to designate Sainovic as Milosevic's man for Kosovo. The Defence will deal first with issues related to the so-called Joint Command. Already now the Defence wishes to stress that the overwhelming majority of evidence used by the Trial Chamber in its analysis relate to 1998, a year that was not charged in the indictment. How does the Trial Chamber reach its conclusions? It cites in detail the content of P1468 and provides explanations of the entries, 306, Volume III, up to 314, Volume III, paragraphs 1 to 13. It cites witnesses who never participated at meetings in Pristina, Crosland, 320, Volume III; Petritsch, and Kickert, 326, Volume III, paras 1 to 18. It cites Cvetic who is contested by all the other witnesses and states that Cvetic is impressive. It cites Cvetic who had no direct insight into what is called the Joint Command because he never attended meetings about he -- which he testified, 315, Volume III, 1 to 14. It cites the telegram where Crosland notes what Dimitrijevic [Realtime transcript read in error "Drewienkiewicz"] said, 320, Volume III. And then the Trial Chamber calls Dimitrijevic to clarify what he had told Crosland, P683. When Dimitrijevic explains what he said, the Trial Chamber rejects everything said by one of only two witnesses that the Trial Chamber invited itself because it obviously does not fit the context of preconceived opinions created by the Trial Chamber, 325, Volume III, paras 1 to 3. A correction to the transcript. The name is not "Drewienkiewicz," it's "Dimitrijevic," General Dimitrijevic. Another witness called by the Chamber is Djakovic, the one who wrote that document, P1468, so that he should clarify. But although it does not say that Djakovic lacks credibility, 330, Volume III, unlike Dimitrijevic, the Chamber rejects all Djakovic's clarifications regarding P1468, paras 1 to 13. The Trial Chamber accepts one-half of Gajic's evidence and rejects the second half given the next day on the same matters, 318, Volume III, paras 2 to 5. The Trial Chamber ignores all the other obvious and proven issues that indicate that Sainovic's role lack the characteristics of key role. The Trial Chamber ignores its own conclusions, including the existence and functioning of all chains of command that there is a Supreme Defence Council which exists, operates, and makes decisions; that there is a plan to combat terrorism in 1998 that is adopted at the highest level; there is a directive of the Chief of General Staff, Grom 98. There are 20 witnesses heard in the case that confirm the chain of command was intact. I repeat, the Supreme Defence Council consists of Milutinovic, Milosevic, and Djukanovic, not Sainovic. The Trial Chamber therefore concludes, based on witness -- on the evidence of witnesses on matters on which they had no direct knowledge nor could they have first-hand knowledge and based on its own interpretations of several written pieces of evidence. When the Chamber invites the authors of these documents to testify and explain their content, the Chamber rejects all their authentic clarifications and explanations. The Trial Chamber in its own analysis seeks to find evidence that would -- should a document -- Sainovic's role in Kosovo and finds only a few. The first is a meeting of 29 October 1998, where reports are made by Pavkovic, Lukic, and Minic. Sainovic does not take part in that meeting; he only briefly talks about the OSCE mission. Then there is a meeting of 5 November 1998, where Milutinovic, who is acquitted of all charges, speaks, explains, instructs, and Sainovic says nothing. Milutinovic is acquitted, although he spoke, explained, and instructed. Sainovic is convicted although he just sat in on this meeting and this meeting is treated as evidence of his key role. Finally, in 1999 the Chamber establishes Sainovic's participation at four meetings. The war lasted from March to June. The evidence speaks to one meeting in April, two in May, and one in June. The substance of these meetings is of no value if one is seeking grounds to conclude that Sainovic played a key role or that he played a role as political co-ordinator. The war with NATO and the war with the KLA require that the co-ordinator of an army and police that are at war hold tens of meetings every day, not four meetings in three months. What did Sainovic co-ordinate in 1999? Who did he co-ordinate? In which way did he co-ordinate? What are the consequences of his co-ordination on the ground or in relation to any crime? Is there an action or operation that was co-ordinated by Sainovic? Not a word about that, not a shred of evidence, not even an assumption. The Trial Chamber ignored its elementary obligation to explain each and every finding. The meeting at which he speaks about the OSCE mission from October 1998, the meeting where he doesn't say anything in November 1998, and four meetings held during the three months of war, during which he does not convey any orders, does not issue orders, did not issue any instructions, on the basis of such evidence there is no reasonable trier of fact who could accept that Sainovic is a key person and - I repeat once again - a political co-ordinator. This is a term that was never clarified. What is particularly controversial is the finding of the Chamber that Sainovic conveys Milosevic's orders. This conclusion is based on a single sentence from P1996, where Sainovic is quoted as saying that Milosevic heard the reports of the commander of the 3rd Army and the MUP staff for Kosovo and that a public release was issued which constitutes a directive and an order of the Supreme Command. It is a point of interest that Slobodan Milosevic died eight years ago on this day. Everything that Sainovic did is indicate this public statement, this release, from the meeting of the commander of the 3rd Army and the leader of the MUP staff at Milosevic's. Even more importantly, at the time when this release was made it had already been given to the members of the MUP. Already on the 6th of May, 1999, this information was -- that is mentioned in the context of Sainovic was submitted to the secretariats of MUP and Kosovo on the 7th of May, 1999. That is 5D1289. The Defence would like to note that the only evidence in the judgement that indicates that Sainovic is conveying Milosevic's orders is precisely the one that Sainovic indicated this news article. The Trial Chamber in its analysis was not in a position to indicate any other part of the evidence that would suggest anything similar to that. All the rest is merely in the sphere of assumption in terms of the relationship between Sainovic and Milosevic. There is not a single reasonable trier of fact for whom an indication of a news article would replace necessary evidence on a key connection that Milosevic had with Sainovic in terms of the forces in Kosovo according to the Trial Chamber. Also at the meeting held on the 17th of May, 1999, Sainovic played a role that was more than marginal. At the meeting Sainovic makes a few comments in passing, whereas others are discussing the essence of the problem of course in accordance with obligations and responsibilities they had with regard to the situation in Kosovo. The conclusion that Sainovic is the key link between Milosevic and Kosovo is something that a reasonable trier of fact can find only if there is evidence on communication between Sainovic and Milosevic and Sainovic the forces of the Army of Yugoslavia and MUP and Kosovo. However, there should also be an absence of evidence that Milosevic had available numerous other channels of communication. However, what is the only thing that does exist in the evidence in this case? Evidence regarding communication between Sainovic and Milosevic at the time relevant to the indictment. Three meetings, two of which were about ten minutes long. What was discussed at these meetings? What, if anything, did Sainovic say to Milosevic or Milosevic to Sainovic? There is no evidence with regard to that whatsoever. Then, evidence about communication between Sainovic and the VJ and MUP in Kosovo, two meetings in the MUP, one meeting with the representatives of VJ and MUP at the very end of the war after all the events that are referred to in the judgement. I repeat, he took part in these meetings very briefly. He came, he exchanged greetings, and he left. As far as evidence is concerned about the communication between Milosevic and the VJ and MUP, things are completely different. There are hundreds of combat reports, orders, directives, a great deal of testimony, and all of that with the absence of any evidence on any kind of obstruction in this communication. Is there any evidence that Sainovic is issuing any kind of orders or communicating in this way? Also, what is unreasonable is to conclude that Sainovic was sent to Kosovo on a one-day mission to -- which was a fact-finding mission and that he enjoys Milosevic's trust as if the president of the state has a single source of information regarding the key problem in the state as if the president of the state has only a single man of confidence. Now, what does the Trial Chamber do? They deny everything that can be concluded on the basis of documents and testimony because Bulatovic is not the only possible authority -- source of authority of Sainovic is Milosevic, and Sainovic is just one of the five deputy prime ministers and Bulatovic is prime minister. The Trial Chamber does not make a distinction between evidence and fact and what are mere impressions. Also, what are all the possibilities for reaching conclusions? Were they properly analysed? Were they excluded? What is the principle in dubio pro reo? That is something that exists in European law and that is something that first-year law students know. Also, it is -- is it possible to conclude on the basis of probability that there is liability? Also, is there any proof of what Milosevic is, what his role is, or is it possible to establish that without any facts in evidence. With regard to the position of Sainovic and his relationship with Milosevic, the Trial Chamber judges on the basis of prejudice about Milosevic and prejudice about Sainovic. That is not done by any reasonable trier of fact. About Sainovic who makes decisions and influences events, that is something that Witnesses Naumann and Vollebaek testified about and they came for the implementation of the agreement of the verification commission -- mission the OSCE in the autumn of 1999, and they take part in talks with Sainovic who heads the commission for co-operation with that mission. They speak about their impressions and they come for this co-operation with the OSCE. They don't know anything about the Army of Yugoslavia, about the MUP, about relations in Serbia and the FRY. They have impressions but they don't have knowledge. Impressions are not a basis for a reasonable trier of fact to reach certain findings. Ciaglinski, a lieutenant-colonel, never met a single member of the Government of the FRY or Serbia. He doesn't know anything about the work of this government, doesn't know anything about the relations within that government. This witness says: I only could have imagined that only Milosevic was above Sainovic. Again, an assumption. The intuition of any witness is not a basis for reaching a conclusion. After all, Milosevic wanted to be above all of us, not only above Sainovic. Maisonneuve saw Sainovic only once at a meeting that was attended by several people. The meeting was chaired by Keller. He did not have any direct knowledge about the position and role of Sainovic. Petritsch and Byrnes also speak about Sainovic, but the Trial Chamber quotes part of their testimony where they present impressions; however, when they speak about the substance of work and the activity of Sainovic when they explain what their co-operation with Sainovic was like, that is something that the Trial Chamber ignores. A first impression is not sufficient and content and explanations are not of relevance. That is the evidence of Sainovic's authority and influence over events, impressions and assumptions, not a shred of evidence. You will allow me a bit of a digression. Mr. Petritsch spoke about the role of Milan Milutinovic. Had Mr. Petritsch said about Sainovic what he said about Milutinovic, Sainovic would be serving life today; however, that did not matter, obviously, to the Prosecution or the Trial Chamber. I hope that you will carefully read that part. What was this order that Sainovic conveyed from Milosevic about a news article that Sainovic indicated, that is something we've already mentioned? If what is meant is the order on cessation of activities which according to the Trial Chamber Sainovic conveyed at the meeting held on the 1st of June, 1999, it is impossible that Sainovic could have conveyed the order on withdrawal as a consequence of an agreement which had not even been concluded at that point in time. The agreement between Milosevic and Ahtisaari is in the case file and it was concluded on the 4th of June, 1999. I repeat, on the 1st of June, 1999, Sainovic was at a meeting. Four days later, Ojdanic authorised senior officers of the VJ to negotiate withdrawal with NATO and the Military Technical Agreement was concluded only on the 9th of June, 1999, so the Trial Chamber ascribes to Sainovic an order which could not have even existed. They ascribe to Sainovic action which is in clear discrepancy with the other findings from this same Trial Chamber. How can someone convey an order that is reached on the 9th, how can one convey that on the 1st? The Trial Chamber establishes Sainovic's key role, but nowhere is it established in the evidence which order did Sainovic issue on his own, if any. There is none. Which activity of Sainovic's reflected on what was happening on the ground and how? There is no such thing. Which activity of Sainovic's was -- had the characteristics of a crime? Not a single one. Which activity of Sainovic's was not in keeping with his position of the deputy prime -- federal prime minister or his position of chairman of the commission for co-operation with the OSCE? Not a single one. Regarding Milosevic's trust in Sainovic, in paragraph 292 of the judgement what is heralded is an explanation of that circumstance but that is not referred to at all in the text of the judgement; that is simply because there is no evidence of this kind. There is no evidence regarding any kind of special relationship between Sainovic and Milosevic because such relationship did not exist. On the contrary, there is evidence that refutes any kind of special ties between them. The Defence of Sainovic thinks that there may be a mistake. There is a special relationship between Milutinovic and Milosevic, and now Sainovic is being replaced in that context. Let me go on. Milosevic in negotiations in Rambouillet and on other occasions had his Special Envoy, also a deputy federal prime minister, but his name was Vladan Kutlesic not Nikola Sainovic. Sainovic was marginalised in the socialist party of Serbia. We presented evidence that Sainovic was dismissed from the position of vice-president of the SPS in 1997. If he was that close to him, he wouldn't have dismissed him. Milosevic proposes that there be a Working Group of the Socialist Party of Serbia, he also proposes a chairman of this Working Group, and Sainovic is not even a member of that group, let alone the leader of that group. Milosevic proposes Milutinovic to be president of Serbia, not Sainovic, thereby also member of the Supreme Defence Council. He keeps Milutinovic at all high positions in the Socialist Party of Serbia, but for the Trial Chamber that was not proof of closeness as opposed to the Sainovic case. Why the Defence wonders? Because Milutinovic in his interview to the OTP said to his wife that at the time when all of this happened he confided that he did not agree with Milosevic. That is the only evidence that they -- that they adduce. Milutinovic was not -- had Milutinovic opposed Milosevic, there would have been no war, had he contradicted him in 1998, none of this would have happened. And confiding in his wife that he disagreed with Milosevic? That was sufficient for the Trial Chamber to conclude Milutinovic is not close to Milosevic. Throughout the war, Milutinovic -- throughout the state of war, Milutinovic was at the command post with his wife and Milosevic was with his wife. They were next door day and night, 78 days except when he went to Kosovo. Sainovic throughout the state of war had two or three meetings with Milosevic that have already been mentioned, but not in private quarters and not in the presence of wives. However, the Trial Chamber acquits Milutinovic because he's not close and convicts Sainovic because he is close. This is just a telling example of the double standards that are applied by the Trial Chamber when assessing closeness with Milosevic. A reasonable trier of fact uses reasonable criteria and bases conclusions on facts, disregarding opinions of witnesses, assumptions, and impressions. With regard to the position of Sainovic and his position of authority, everything is just an opinion, an impression; there is no evidence whatsoever to that effect. After all, you will see that the police was subordinated to Milutinovic, not Sainovic, because the police is Serbian and Sainovic was in the federal government. The existence of a Joint Command and the nature of a Joint Command. An explanation as to who needs a Joint Command is provided by the Trial Chamber through Dimitrijevic, but through an erroneous and incorrect interpretation of Dimitrijevic. Although Dimitrijevic only speaks about Pavkovic's action in relation to the VJ, the Trial Chamber understands that as a way of co-ordinating between the VJ and the police. However, Dimitrijevic makes no reference to the police. He says that he's speculating when testifying about the Joint Command. I do apologise. I do apologise. It's elderly people who get the flu first. As I've already said, Dimitrijevic does not refer to the police at all. He, himself, says that he is speculating as regards Joint Command; however, this does not prevent the Trial Chamber from basing on Dimitrijevic their conclusion that there is a Joint Command for ensuring better co-ordination between the army and the police. A reasonable trier of fact cannot construe evidence in that way and then base findings on that. The Trial Chamber finds on the basis of positions of the witness in a different context - and that is that he himself says it's speculation - they base their findings on that and they are ignoring consistent evidence about the co-ordination of VJ and MUP actions in 1998. When talking about the content of Joint Command, the Chamber ignores the following participants: Minic, Matkovic, Andjelkovic, Djakovic, that have already been called by the Trial Chamber. And he says that these are not the kind of documents that the OTP says, and he says that he and Pavkovic created the name of the meeting as Joint Command. The Chamber ignores the testimony of Mijatovic, Vucurevic, Adamovic, and they only trust Cvetic who was not there and who did not see any of that. The Chamber considers 40 witnesses who are explaining Joint Command, and the conclusion they reach about the nature of Joint Command is similar only to the testimony of a single witness, this notorious Cvetic. Why doesn't the Chamber appreciate what more than 40 witnesses say about the nature of the Joint Command? Why don't they trust them? Why don't they explain this? Why do they trust only Cvetic? I repeat, he was not there. He did not see this. He had no idea about any of this. This position taken by the Trial Chamber is flagrant ignoring of evidence and accepting assumptions as facts. You know, my professor of law - this was a long time ago, half a century ago - he said a sentence that stands forever, that all the assumptions in this world fall if you have a shred of evidence. And the Chamber does the opposite: They are ignoring evidence and trusting assumptions. The Chamber explains with a single sentence their findings on the authority of the Joint Command. Their meetings were more than a daily exchange of information. This position is a telling example of this impermissible imprecision in reaching conclusions more than an exchange, but what is this more? What was said? What was ordered? What was done? What happened? If a reasonable trier of fact says that it is not an exchange of information but it's more than that, they have an obligation to say what this more is. So this is a serious mistake of the Trial Chamber. Conclusions about the authority of this Joint Command over the VJ and the MUP is something that the Trial Chamber bases on a few examples from 1998. All of these examples are untenable. They all show that lines of subordination have been kept. I do apologise once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, counsel, could I ask you a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please explain to me the relationship between the Joint Command and the so-called Working Group. Is that Working Group created to co-ordinate the relationship between VJ and MUP? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you look at the indictment, at the beginning it is claimed that there was a meeting of the Socialist Party of Serbia and that that joint plan was made there. That was what the Prosecution claimed. When the Working Group was established at the proposal of Slobodan Milosevic, Minic as its head and two ministers as its members, the minister of sport and the ministry of industry. The goal of the Working Group was to go on a one-day visit and to see what was going on. That was the interest of the leading party, to see what was going on on the ground. In order to see all that, you have to bear in mind the specificities of Yugoslavia. The army was a joint system, whereas the police belonged to just one republic. And in order to see what was going on, the socialist party sent its party delegation to inspect the situation on the ground. And as for the communications in the Joint Command, those were the people who were there, who had to negotiate, who had to be informed, because there was civilian structures there as well, the Red Cross, local bodies of Serb government and various ties with the international community. There was television there, they could watch the news, and they could exchange information. That was an exchange of information, but that has nothing to do with the commission that reported back to Milosevic as to what they had established. Sainovic joined them because the federal state had to send somebody to be kept abreast and Sainovic went there on Bulatovic's order and he also went back there occasionally in 1998. What is important for the Joint Command is that the lines of command in the police and the army were not rendered uncapable and there is no influence on the command. I don't know whether you are satisfied with my answer. So there were lines of command, they were not rendered disabled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the role of the Joint Command? There is an example of the request for helicopters which was made by Sainovic for the Red Cross. It is the General Staff and the command of the 3rd Army that allows the use of helicopters and this was not approved. If Sainovic was that important, he would have been given the helicopter for the Red Cross. When it comes to the deployment of combat groups, combat groups were deployed exclusively pursuant to the orders of the command of the 3rd Army. At that time, the accused Pavkovic was the commander of the Pristina Corps, the commander of the 3rd Army was in Nis, that was General Samardzic, and those two approved all those activities. For example, the implementation of rapid intervention forces. Those forces were never established. There was an exchange of thoughts and opinions, but those forces were never established. The example of the implementation of the third phase of the plan. Irrespective of Pavkovic's attempts, the units of the Pristina Corps were not used if there was no order by the command of the 3rd Army and that person was Pavkovic's superior. When it comes to the Perisic -- letter, P717, Perisic speaks exclusively about attempts to influence the use of corps units which was never materialised. The example of orders by the Pristina Corps, the Trial Chamber concluded that the operation was under the control of the command of the Pristina Corps; and that is P1427 and P1428. The Trial Chamber accepted that the chain of command within the Army of Yugoslavia was preserved. The example of orders where approval by the Joint Command is sought, it is accepted by the Trial Chamber that in reality the approvals were issued by the command of the Pristina Corps and not of the Joint Command. The Joint Command during the period of 1999. The conclusions of the Joint Command during 1999 are dramatically different from the conclusions about the Joint Command in 1998. The Trial Chamber says the existence of the Joint Command is less visible. The evidence is less detailed, less precise. There are no minutes of any of the meetings. The evidence on Joint Command is superficial. There is no evidence on a clear mandate of the Joint Command in 1999. Orders which bear the title of the Joint Command are actually the orders which were created at the Pristina Corps. Everything that exists is a conclusion by the Trial Chamber based on Vasiljevic, that a meeting that took place on the 1st of June, 1999, was similar to the meetings that were held in 1998. The only similarity that does exist is that that meeting was held in Kosovo and that the topic of the meeting was the situation in Kosovo. Everything else is different. The participants were not the same as in 1998. There was no continuity. If it served co-ordination, then one meeting was not enough. No minutes were taken. There were no conclusions. There were no civilians. The similarity that was established by the Trial Chamber does not constitute grounds for a reasonable trier of fact to make inferences about facts. Similar is not the same. One similar differs from another similar by definition. The Trial Chamber cannot adhere to the conclusion that something was similar. Either it was a meeting of the Joint Command or it wasn't. If it was only similar, one cannot use similarities to draw conclusions that have far-reaching repercussions on criminal responsibility. You will remember if it walks like a duck, it acts like a duck, it's a duck, but it's not always the case. The Trial Chamber says that some of the accused mentioned a Joint Command in 1999, and by mentioning it they evoked the whole system of co-ordination that existed in 1998. Again, no explanation. What does it mean when somebody says "mention"? Does the body exist or does it not exist? And does the body change if the situation exists on the ground or not? The Trial Chamber says that the Pristina Corps used the title "Joint Command" in order to gain authority in its orders or more authority. What does it mean when one says "more authority"? Who needed that? The VJ units are anyway under the command of the Pristina Corps. The Trial Chamber states that the MUP did not receive orders by the Pristina Corps, but just excerpts from the maps. So the logic of the Trial Chamber leads to the conclusion that the Pristina Corps doesn't have authority in its own units and that it can gain it only if it -- title is served Joint Command. However, this is a conclusion that a reasonable trier of fact cannot accept. Very important. Mentioning the Joint Command is a very important factor because when it comes to the planning and implementation it evokes the authority that existed in 1998. This is just one in a series of unclear and contradictory conclusions. Did the body exist in the reality or did it exist because it was mentioned? For example, one could say that Sainovic died and only [indiscernible] could exercise authority. Did that -- did the accused play a role in that body? The conclusion of the Trial Chamber that the Joint Command was established in order to allow MUP commanders to save face and not to be under the command of the Army of Yugoslavia before and during the state of emergency, this serves a special explanation. This is just an assumption. Why would Milosevic need Pavkovic and the Joint Command when there were decisions of the superior bodies and commands for the use of the Army of Yugoslavia? Why would Milosevic need Pavkovic or Sainovic or Joint Command to co-ordinate with the MUP when there were uninterrupted chains of command in the MUP? And when it comes to President Milutinovic, they were together every day from breakfast to when they went to bed, and Milutinovic was in charge of the police. Why would Milosevic need Pavkovic if Milosevic was a politician who acts without any control, either by the parliament or party, who was described as a politician who could appoint, dismiss, or demote any officer or official anywhere within the state structure? If he could enjoy Milutinovic's support to make a decision on the removal of General Perisic on the 24th of November, 1998, and if he -- and Milutinovic could have prevented that if he did not agree. If he could make a decision on the removal of the commander of the 3rd Army, Dusan Samardzic, on the 25th of December, 1998, if pursuant to the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Law on The Army he was authorised and in charge of the personnel policy in the Army of Yugoslavia, then it is absolutely unclear why he would be afraid of those changes, why he would create special bodies. Why did he need Pavkovic in order to bypass officers who did not agree with the use of the Army of Yugoslavia? He could have made changes in line with the constitution in a very simple, legal, and fast way. He could change people, he could remove people if they were not like-minded and if they existed and if they represented a problem for the use of the units of the Army of Yugoslavia. That is why the conclusions of the Trial Chamber are not logical, they were not -- they are not grounded on the facts and the Defence deems them as conclusions on the facts that no reasonable trier of fact could arrive at.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please be asked to slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that is the time for the break and we will have a break for 15 minutes. Then we will resume at 11.00 sharp. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fila, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. When the allegation from the indictment became moot that the Joint Command headed by its commander Sainovic was in command of the military and the police in Kosovo in 1992, what also became moot was the modus operandi --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I'm sorry to interrupt you. Judge Guney has a question. Judge Guney has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Counsel, before we resume, I have a question in the framework of the Joint Command and Working Group. Is the role given by the Trial Chamber to the Working Group compatible with its conclusion on the Joint Command? This is the first half of the question. Because according to Stojanovic, the Trial Chamber found that the Working Group was established to represent the Joint Command or part of it. This finding, is it erroneous as the Working Group for the separate entity with separate authorities? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your conclusion is absolutely correct. The Working Group which was established by Slobodan Milosevic attended the meeting of the Socialist Party of Serbia and it had a party task because that was the ruling party in our parliament at the time, and it consisted of three top officials of the Socialist Party who were also members of the government, Matkovic and Andjelkovic, as well as the president of the Federal Assembly, Milomir Minic. That Working Group went there to see what was happening in Kosovo, to report back to the party, and that is why the conclusion that the Joint Command is totally different from the Working Group is completely correct. The two are not the same. It was only later when they returned, seven days later, and reported back to Slobodan Milosevic on what they had seen, that they were given a task to go there occasionally and to gather information and report back to the party as to what was going on. In other words, the meetings of the Joint Command were one thing and the Working Group consisting of three people is a different thing. Especially if you look at the notes drafted by the Joint Command, you will see that the three of them were not there together. Nikola Sainovic that I represent was the representative of the federal state; he had nothing whatsoever to do with that Working Group. I don't know whether I have made myself clear. They gathered in a place where they had television to watch CNN and the rest and that's where they exchanged experiences. Every one of them did their own thing. The Working Group was sent there to see what was going on and to report back to their own party as to what was going on in Kosovo. Sainovic represented the federal government and negotiated with NATO and the security organisation. Everybody did their own work. It was like a club; however, there was no efficient command because there was no commander. You know what an army is like: If there is no commander, there is no command, no orders are issued. When the allegation from the indictment became moot that the Joint Command headed by its commander, Sainovic, commanded the military and the police in Kosovo in 1999, what also became moot was the modus operandi of the role played by Sainovic according to the Prosecutor. If there was no Joint Command which commanded, then there was no Sainovic. If the Prosecutor's allegation on the Joint Command became moot, what also became moot was the explanation for the participation of Nikola Sainovic in the developments in 1999. There is -- there was no Joint Command, Sainovic was not a commander. What was he? That cannot be replaced by a change and by the introduction of a new term, the political co-ordinator. The person who was accused as the commander of the Joint Command was found guilty as a political co-ordinator. We discussed that, we did not explain the term, no evidence was presented to that effect. The following chapter is the significant contribution to the JCE, 2-1 and 2-2. The Defence does not deny that the Trial Chamber established correctly that when it comes to the joint criminal enterprise, that the accused has to be demonstrated to have made a significant contribution to the JCE. However, the Defence in its appeal brief points to a number of reasons why Sainovic's engagement in Kosovo in the course of 1999 could not be seen as significant. The Trial Chamber states that Sainovic is the man whom Milosevic used to orchestrate developments in Kosovo, another new term, and that Sainovic provided his own instructions, all with a view for Serbia to keep control over Kosovo. Who did he give instructions to? What instructions? We never saw that. With all due respect, the Defence concludes that this conclusion reached by the Trial Chamber is unreasonable. This conclusion denies the fact that there was a state, that there were institutions. The Trial Chamber treats Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as Milosevic's private turf, where he has free and unlimited decision power, where he can deploy people and issue orders. Especially impressive is the conclusion of the Trial Chamber which permeates the entire decision. Milosevic's position and role does not have to be proven. Milosevic's position was given in advance and notorious; everybody knew what it was. The Trial Chamber in the case file has some evidence about conversations between the highest-ranking state officials. However, the Trial Chamber treats these conversations as private conversations that the omnipotent Milosevic has with his yes-men. The Trial Chamber treats these conversations as something that was happening outside of the system and that was contrary to the constitution and the laws. In this decision, political conversations are treated as conversations which are not taking place in public, and thus they represent conspiracy to commit crime, as if there were a political system in the world where there are no conversations between state officials that take place outside of the Assembly, outside of the government, outside of the public. The work of no Assembly in the world is completely transparent. The Trial Chamber says that Milosevic - and I quote - "orchestrates events." And it wants to represent Milosevic's authority as something that exists outside of the system, as if Milosevic exercised his own will through some of his men beyond and above the constitution. Milosevic's authority is a fact, but that authority stems from the fact that Milosevic was the president of the FRY, that he was the number one man of the Supreme Defence Council of the FRY, and that he was also the leader of the leading political party in the FRY and in Serbia. The way and extent of Milosevic's influence on the position, the role, of Sainovic as a high-ranking state official can be interpreted only in that context which is typical of every state organisation and which does not constitute conspiracy to commit crime. As I already told you, members of the Supreme Defence Council were Milosevic, as the president of Yugoslavia, the president of Montenegro, and the president of Serbia, Mr. Milutinovic, for whom the Trial Chamber established that he was not close to Milosevic. The Trial Chamber bases its conclusion that Sainovic was the person that Milosevic used to orchestrate events in Kosovo, uses to show that Sainovic's role within the context of the implementation of the joint criminal enterprise was significant because the significance is the key. The Trial Chamber, however, mystifies the position and role of Sainovic. It qualifies it as a man who Milosevic gave the Kosovo brief as Milosevic's man for Kosovo, as the person who was in charge of operations on the daily basis, and these are all quotes. The Trial Chamber does not try and explain and analyse Sainovic's activities of which evidence can be found in the case file. It does not try to analyse activities for which there is proof that they can be ascribed to Sainovic. It does not analyse where Sainovic was in the course of 1999. The Trial Chamber moves at the level of prejudices and assumptions which, however, is not enough for any reasonable trier of facts which wants to take position on the existence or nonexistence of criminal responsibility. When you look at the evidence. When you do away with empty allegations about the person for Kosovo orchestration and the Kosovo brief, and when all that is reduced to the level of available evidence, Sainovic's role for every reasonable trier of fact imposes itself as the role that is within constitutional and legal authorities that determine Sainovic's position as a government representative in charge of international relations. There are several clearly separate tasks that Sainovic was in charge of with regard to Kosovo. At first, in the summer of 1991 -- 1998, pursuant to a decision of the president of the federal government, Bulatovic, Sainovic was sent to Kosovo as the vice prime minister in charge of foreign affairs. The second phase started after the October Agreement that was signed by Holbrooke and Milosevic. When Sainovic was proposed by the federal ministry of foreign affairs and appointed by the federal government as the president of the committee on co-operation with the Kosovo verification commission. The third phase was Sainovic's participation at the Rambouillet conference where Andjelkovic proposed and the government of the Republic of Serbia established a decision on the composition of the delegation and Sainovic is one of its 12 members. And finally, Sainovic participated in the Rugova proceedings and that was entrusted to him by the president of the federal government. Therefore, Sainovic's tasks were not mystified or castration of events in Kosovo. They were rather legitimate activities within the system of the state administration of the FRY and Serbia, were envisaged by the law and by the constitution and all the actors including prime ministers, presidents of parties, presidents of the republics. They participate and they exercise their influence. And on all of that, there is written evidence for Sainovic to be where he was supposed to be and what his tasks were. We have to pay a lot of attention to Sainovic's activities after the 24th of March, 1999. There is not a single shred of evidence testifying to the fact that Sainovic carried out some sort of co-ordination of forces and activities, that he provided instructions or suggestions, that his instructions and suggestions in any way influenced the developments on the ground, the movements and activities of the units there, and especially not in the phase of the implementation of the goal to exercise control over Kosovo, and the last part of the sentence was a quote. All of that is particularly emphasised by the Defence and all of that refers to the period after the 24th of March, 1999, at the time when crimes had already happened and that were established by the first-instance judgement. The Trial Chamber has before it proof on the ways the Army of Yugoslavia and the MUP were commanded and controlled. There is no single shred of evidence that in the process of command and control there was influence of anybody beyond those who were envisaged to exercise control in the chain of command, including Sainovic, especially in the period after the departure of the Kosovo Verification Mission and the beginning of the war with NATO and the KLA. The Trial Chamber was not in a position in its arguments to point to a single piece of evidence that would indicate Sainovic's activity and his influence on the events on the ground, especially after the departure of the KVM. To judge Sainovic's contribution to the JCE as significant, evidence is necessary that Sainovic influenced the events and the way this enterprise was implemented and that his significant contribution existed. The Defence at this point wants especially to point out one sentence that we can find in paragraph 467, Volume III, of the judgement which shows the extent of the error committed by the Trial Chamber when it was assessing and making conclusions on Sainovic. The Trial Chamber admits that there is much less evidence of the direct involvement of Sainovic regarding 1999 than 1998, but that some evidence exists. And the Trial Chamber indicates as such evidence his attendance of meetings. We have already discussed his attendance of meetings, four meetings in three months. The Trial Chamber, however, asked for the opinion of this Defence team, and the Trial Chamber - in the view of this Defence - was required to analyse the content of these meetings independently and autonomously of the meetings that Sainovic attended in 1998 [as interpreted]. What kind of meetings were they? What did Sainovic say at these meetings? Can his words be qualified by any reasonable interpretation as giving orders or orchestration? Did his words have any effect or consequence on the events on the ground? Did, as a consequence of what Sainovic say, a military or a police unit move? Was any action taken? Was a crime perpetrated? There is nothing. There are just four meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: May I ask you a clarification, counsel. Are you speaking about the meetings in 1998 or 1999? Because the transcript says "1998," so I don't know what is the position -- or referring to 1999, just to know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the meetings in 1999. There were four. And the point is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and the point is to prove the difference between the meetings in 1998 and 1999. When you look at the minutes, the transcripts, of these meetings you will see the extent to which Sainovic was present at all and what he said. In the context of Sainovic's significant role in the implementation of the JCE, the Trial Chamber places him in the context of Joint Command in 1999; however, concerning that Joint Command in 1999, that same Trial Chamber states that the evidence is unclear, insufficient, that there is no information of its mandate in 1999. At one point the Trial Chamber states that the Joint Command in 1999 in fact evokes its authority from 1998, whatever that means. In the absence of evidence concerning 1999, the Trial Chamber impermissibly uses analogy and projects conclusions concerning 1998 to the period in 1999, that is to say the period when the criminal acts established were committed. In my country, criminal law prohibits the method of analogy, that is the case in Serbia. In civil law and in lawsuits, it is used but not in criminal law. The Trial Chamber has no proof that Sainovic participated in any co-ordination in 1999. The Trial Chamber has no evidence of the existence of the Joint Command in 1999 either. Instead, it depicts the existence of that alleged body through impressions and memories of 1998. The Trial Chamber completely ignores key differences between 1998 and 1999, whereas these differences are of decisive importance for any conclusions on this issue. In 1998 in my country there was peace. In 1999 there was a state of war in my country. In 1999 my country was at war with NATO. There is a difference between 1998, gentlemen, and 1999; the difference is war, the difference is NATO. It's no small difference. And therefore, there is a considerable impact on the nature of conflict, and that is why in 1999 there are no civilians attending any meetings with members of the VJ and the MUP because in a state of war there can be no civilians involved in any country, including mine. The Trial Chamber commits a grave error of law in establishing facts because it uses analogy as a means to derive evidence by virtue of concluding things about a certain time-period based on findings that apply to a completely different time. We, the Defence, believe that by this submission we respond in a slightly broader context to one of the questions posed by the Appeal Chamber on page 3 of the order of 20th February, 2013. The actus reus and mens rea of Mr. Sainovic in the events that he's charged with are established exclusively by analogy. All the conclusions about his actions and intent were formed by the Trial Chamber by analysing facts from 1998. Concerning 1998 the Trial Chamber establishes Sainovic's authority and its source. Concerning 1998 the Trial Chamber establishes there were some meetings discussing activities of the army and the police and that some of these meetings were attended by Sainovic. Concerning 1998, the Trial Chamber establishes the existence of the Joint Command and its jurisdiction, while establishing Sainovic's alleged role. All these things are missing in 1999 and this is the period for which Sainovic is charged. We don't know whether the Joint Command existed then or not. There are only memories that are evoked for certain reasons. We don't know where and what Sainovic was co-ordinating. We don't know whether he was giving any sensible or significant orders or instructions because we don't know where he was at all at the time of the indictment. There is only information that in the relevant time he attended four meetings. In my country, the difference between 1998 and 1999 is the state of war and the NATO attack. The Trial Chamber simply has no evidence for 1999, and in a very impermissible way it uses analogy and makes conclusions and concludes that if something happened in 1998 it must have happened also in 1999. This is a serious violation of the fundamental principle of dubio pro reo. This is a gross violation of due process against Sainovic. At this point the Defence believes that it is pertinent also to respond to the second part of question from the distinguished Appeals Chamber relating to 1998. This Defence is required to state its position as to whether mens rea in this accused may be established under JCE I, specifically deportation and forced transfer based on the accused's knowledge of crimes committed in 1998, including crimes that are not deportation or forced transfer. The Defence would like first to deal with the facts. In paragraph 920, Volume I, of the trial judgement it is said that with a few exceptions, generally speaking, the evidence led is not of such nature as to be able to prove specific criminal acts committed by individual groups of VJ or MUP forces in 1998. In certain cases there was disproportionate use of force causing grave consequences and certain observers did express their concern. The Trial Chamber analyses Sainovic's knowledge of the said crimes in 1998 in paragraphs from 441 to 443, Volume III. The existence of refugees amidst fighting in 1998 is no proof of crimes; it is proof of the seriousness of the conflict that existed in Kosovo at that time. It seems that the Trial Chamber wants to represent the appearance of refugees in 1998 as a harbinger of deportations that allegedly existed in 1998; however, in evidence for 1998 there is no trace of that. The appearance of refugees and deportation and forcible transfers have no common elements and cannot be compared for the purpose of Sainovic's knowledge of alleged crimes. The Trial Chamber also cites the example of Gornje Obrinje, 899, Volume I. Concerning the events in Obrinje, the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia required a report. The command of the Pristina Corps informed the General Staff that they have no information of any massacre in Gornje Obrinje. A Finnish forensic team was supposed to conduct an investigation. That team arrived in Kosovo, but due to problems with access and security it did not finalise its job. The investigating judge of the district court in Pristina carried out an investigation in this case. Milomir Minic also agreed there should be an investigation. He was man number two under the speaker of the parliament. The crimes, however, were not established in a way that could be designated as Sainovic's knowledge of crimes from 1998. The events in 1998 that the Trial Chamber calls crimes do not have any similarity to events in 1999 in terms of their basic characteristics, the method of perpetration, the extent, or the circumstances under which they happened. The events from 1998 are not and cannot be represented as knowledge or notice for 1998. Also, knowledge of any crimes in 1998 cannot be used as proof of foreseeability of crimes in 1999 because the alleged crimes are different in all the fundamental elements that characterised them. The standard for the existence of criminal acts of deportation and forcible transfer is that the forcible transfer is from areas where the displaced persons were lawfully residing. In paragraph 919, the Trial Chamber establishes that a significant number of persons was displaced, but establishes two different groups of reasons: The fighting between FRY and Serbia forces against the KLA and the disproportionate use of force in certain areas. The Trial Chamber speaks nowhere of forcible transfer. Finally, concerning the act of deportation, there is absolutely no evidence of displacement or transfer across the state border, and at the end of the day all the persons who left their homes in 1998 did return with the help of state organs of Serbia and FRY. In many cases the state helped them to restore their damaged houses and lends assistance in many other ways. There is also evidence of that in the case file. Finding intent for any crime in 1998 is simply impossible, especially in the case of Sainovic. The events from 1998 are fundamentally different from events in 1998 in all of their important elements, which makes any conclusion on the intent of Sainovic in this way impossible. Sainovic's intent. At this point, the Defence wishes to point out especially significant arguments relating to Sainovic's intent to commit the criminal acts with which he is charged. In paragraph 466, Volume III, of the trial judgement, the Trial Chamber found that Sainovic had the intent to forcibly displace part of the Albanian population in Kosovo, and thus affect the ethnic balance in order to ensure permanent control of Serbia and FR Yugoslavia over Kosovo. The Trial Chamber uses five sources in paragraphs 428 to 438, discussing Sainovic's mens rea, these are witnesses Naumann, Phillips, Byrnes, Loncar, and Petritsch. These are persons who at the time relevant for the indictment were in contact with Sainovic, that is, before the conflict occurred. The Trial Chamber analyses Naumann but concludes that his testimony cannot be used as proof of Sainovic's attitude towards the Albanian population in Kosovo. Byrnes was the head of the US diplomatic observer mission in Kosovo. Byrnes states that Sainovic believed the problems in Kosovo should be resolved by political means, that continued work should be done to find a mutually acceptable solution. He also testifies that Sainovic worked to find such a solution, that he was always co-operative, and that he even tried to negotiate with the KLA in order to find that solution. Byrnes who participated in both the negotiations at -- in Rambouillet and other discussions testified that he trusted Sainovic. Petritsch is also cited in that part of the indictment [as interpreted] dealing with Sainovic's intent. This witness states that Sainovic was the most constructive in seeking a solution for the overall situation. Loncar, too, testified that Sainovic advocated forming a multi-ethnic police in Kosovo which is an obvious proof that Sainovic saw that a solution for Kosovo was possible only through agreement and compromise. Petritsch testified that in Rambouillet Milutinovic was the most vociferous criticiser, that he had a very negative influence on the negotiations; however, this means nothing for the Trial Chamber. The Trial Chamber ignores all the reasons indicated by persons who were in direct contact with Sainovic and decides to accept, instead, the testimony of Phillips. Acting in this way, the Trial Chamber takes the road that not a single reasonable trier of fact would take. Byrnes, Loncar, and Petritsch alike were Prosecution witnesses. Byrnes and Petritsch are diplomats, high-ranking diplomats in their countries. Both of them were extremely conversant with the situation in Serbia and they dealt with it for a long time. Their perception, along with Loncar's and other evidence, do not leave any room for the conclusion made by the Chamber. Byrnes and Petritsch are people who spent a lot of time with Sainovic. Their testimony cannot be compared in terms of weight with the testimony of people who saw Sainovic once or never. The Trial Chamber does not explain at all why it does not accept Byrnes and why it ignores Petritsch and Loncar. The Trial Chamber accepts the testimony of Phillips. However, even with regard to Phillips the Trial Chamber does something that not a single reasonable trier of fact would do. It ignores the entire evidence given by Phillips and bases its far-reaching conclusion of Sainovic's intent on one single sentence uttered by Phillips which is taken out of all context and is refuted by the entirety of his testimony. The Trial Chamber accepts Phillips' statement that Albanians do not belong in Kosovo and that Kosovo is a cradle of Serbian civilisation and that Albanians do not want to co-exist with Serbs. The Defence emphasises that Phillips uttered this sentence in a way that is unclear after several repetitions of the same question by the Prosecutor, where the Prosecutor even interrupted the witness and rephrased the question until he finally got the answer he expected. What did Phillips testify to? He testified that Sainovic was sincere when he talked about the co-existence of Serbs and Albanians, that at the meeting on 24 November 1998 Sainovic said that the majority in Kosovo believes it is possible to find a political solution, and he himself was hoping for such a solution, that Sainovic at a meeting with Walker on 8 December 1998 put forward his proposals sincerely in good faith in the desire to resolve problems, that at a meeting with Walker on 14 January 1999 he said he was satisfied with the joint work and that the KLA and the VJ have to look for a political solution, that work should be done on the main element of a mutual agreement. Phillips testified this but he also noted that in his official notebooks that weren't contemporaneous and that were subject to special protection measures in this case. Phillips further testified that Sainovic was in favour of the co-existence of Serbs and Albanians in Kosovo, that he was in favour of a political solution, that Sainovic was hoping that solution was possible, that work should continue on reaching an agreement. The Trial Chamber accepts, however, only one sentence from Witness Phillips, although at least four other situations show a completely different position of Sainovic. If Sainovic was in favour of the co-existence of Serbs and Albanians, if he was in favour of a mutually acceptable solution at negotiations, if he was sincere in his desire to negotiate a solution, that it is -- then it is impossible to accept only one sentence out of the whole testimony, which is on top of everything unclear in form and unclear in context. We should recall, once again, the testimony on Sainovic's role in Rambouillet, where he once again expressed his desire to have problems resolved peaceably. The Defence concludes that not a single reasonable trier of fact would make the conclusion on Sainovic's intent in the way that the Trial Chamber did in this case, ignoring all the witnesses who have direct knowledge, ignoring written evidence that is contemporaneous, ignoring the essence of Phillips' testimony before the Trial Chamber and the decision underlying the conviction of Nikola Sainovic which is based on a single sentence, which is to say the least contradictory to the rest of the testimony of the same witness. Now we will address the Appeals Chamber's question concerning the making of the indictment against Sainovic public. In its order --
