utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. In its order of 20th February 2013, the Appeals Chamber asks the Defence to state its position on the importance of the fact that the indictment against Sainovic was made public on 27 May 1999, whereas the last crime for which Sainovic was convicted happened two days earlier, on 25th May 1999. First of all, the Defence would like to note that the general accessibility of information cannot support a presumption on Sainovic's actual knowledge and awareness. It is only on true knowledge and awareness can one find criminal responsibility. Therefore, accessibility via media cannot be taken as a conclusion on Sainovic's actual awareness of the fact that an indictment was issued against him in the absence of specific evidence about his knowledge, and there is no such knowledge in this case. Also, as noted by the Appeals Chamber as well, the indictment was issued after the crimes for which Sainovic was charged were -- had occurred. Possible knowledge or awareness of the indictment could be of significance only in the context of the possible punishment of perpetrators; however, in the case file there is not a single shred of evidence that would show Sainovic's authority or ability to punish anyone or to discipline anyone. The question of the Trial Chamber has to do with the mens rea standard in relation to the third category of joint criminal enterprise. In relation to the question of the Trial Chamber, how the Defence of Sainovic would be affected in terms of the fourth and fifth grounds of appeal by a possible acceptance of the appeal of the Prosecutor in relation to correcting the mens rea standard in terms of the third category of JCE, the Defence wishes to highlight the following: First of all, the Trial Chamber bases its position on the necessary standard on the ruling of the Appeals Chamber in the Brdjanin case and the Defence presented its response in paragraphs 49 through 56. However, if this Trial Chamber were to find that the standard of probable should be replaced by the standard of possible, the Defence wishes to recall the position of the Appeals Chamber in the Karadzic case concerning the third category of joint criminal enterprise of the 25th of June, 2009, where it says that the standard of probability cannot apply to situations when the accused is considerably far away from what is happening and that mens rea in terms of the third category of joint criminal enterprise requires that there -- that there is a sufficiently substantial ability to have a crime committed so that it could have been foreseen by the accused person. The Defence, however, would wish to highlight that irrespective of legal standard the conclusion would be the same in relation to Sainovic's responsibility for the crimes of murder and damage to military --

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Foreseeable. There is detailed reference in paragraphs 397 to 412 of the indictment. Finally, the incident in Tusilje. It is not contained in the indictment and it is contained in the judgement. Although this incident is not part of the appeal of the Sainovic's Defence, the Defence believes that the Appeals Chamber should certainly acquit Sainovic of any responsibility in view of what happened in Tusilje. And, finally, the decision on sentencing. The Defence is convinced that the arguments that are presented in the appeal convincingly demonstrate that the only just decision in the Sainovic case would be a judgement of acquittal. However, if this honourable Appeals Chamber would not accept the positions of the Defence, the Defence would like to indicate that the Trial Chamber in terms of sentencing made mistakes, and therefore the sentence is totally inadequate. If Sainovic conveyed some information or some instruction, the number of such cases is very small. The Chamber was only able to identify very few such situations. In most events, in a vast number of the activities of the VJ and the MUP, Sainovic's information or instruction constitutes an insignificant part in the hundreds and thousands of orders, reports that were exchanged between the commanders of the VJ, the MUP, and the structures that were superior to them. If there is a role that was played by Sainovic, if there is a contribution rendered by Sainovic, if there is his authority, then his contribution is very small and his authority was seldom used, if ever. If there are four meetings, if there are four ambiguous or unclear instructions that were allegedly conveyed by Sainovic and if at the same time there is a war and a state of war, if there are commands, staffs, communications equipment, orders, reports, and uninterrupted chain of command in the military and the police, if there are organs of civilian government, then Sainovic's role - if any - is minimal and the sentence is excessive. So if this Appeals Chamber were to find that Sainovic is responsible, then certainly the sentence should be much less strict than the one that was pronounced by the Trial Chamber, 22 years in prison for four episodes at the time relevant to the indictment, four episodes of marginal importance, and that is a sentence that no reasonable trier of fact could agree to. Taking into account all these arguments, the Defence appeals to the Appeals Chamber to take into account all arguments, assess the facts and the legal aspects of the appeal, and to view all the mistakes that were made by the Trial Chamber and to reach a lawful and just judgement. In the view of this Defence, it can only be a judgement of acquittal of Nikola Sainovic. In the time that remains, I would like to say something. This is a year in which the Tribunal is commemorating 20 years of its existence. Many persons since then have left, we should remember them, we should remember their contribution. I would particularly like to note Professor Antonio Cassese, who unfortunately is no longer with us. Many persons gave their contribution here and I believe that we should remember all of them. In that spirit, I wish to paraphrase the words of Nelson Mandela, the greatest living fighter for human rights, who said that each and every one of us leaves traces of what they did, they continue in time, and without any error they show the path that we had taken, whether we took the path of truth and justice or the other path. We each choose our own path. I ask the distinguished Appeals Chamber to agree to the road of justice and to acquit my client, Nikola Sainovic. Today negotiations between the state of Serbia and the Kosovo Albanians start and the Serbian delegation includes the president, the prime minister, and the deputy prime minister, and this is of decisive importance for all of the events involved. If all of that were true, if others had been accused in Serbia, not only the president and the three chiefs of General Staff, then we would not have had the situation that we have now. However, many things remained unpunished. The bombing of the Chinese embassy, then also the exodus of Serbian refugees from Kosovo. Had people been found guilty for that, today we would have said that the third objective of this Tribunal would have been achieved, that is to say to reach reconciliation among the peoples of the region. Had that happened, we could say proudly today we have achieved that third objective as well. Thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Fila. I believe that you are far ahead of your time allocated to you. Well, could we hear the submissions from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will respond to Mr. Sainovic's challenges to the joint criminal enterprise and its operation, including the system for co-ordinating the activities of the VJ and MUP, which included the Joint Command. Given the interconnected nature of many of the issues that will be discussed over the course of the week, my response submissions will also try to provide context to the findings as they relate to Mr. Pavkovic and Lukic as members of the joint criminal enterprise and, in part, Mr. Lazarevic. My colleagues, Ms. Martin Salgado and Ms. Monchy, will answer the questions that relate to Mr. Sainovic as set out in Your Honour's order of 31 January 2013 and respond to the issues relating to actus reus and mens rea respectively. Your Honour, Mr. Sainovic brings few allegations of legal error, and as is evident from his brief and his remarks today, the vast majority of his challenges are alleged factual errors. In his arguments, he repeatedly criticises the Trial Chamber's decision-making by citing to other evidence in the record and suggesting other conclusions should have been drawn. As our response brief sets out in detail, a large number of his submissions meet the grounds for summary dismissal and the same holds true for the submissions of the other appellants. We do not consider it would be of assistance to Your Honours for us to address such arguments in oral submission this week, and if we have not responded specifically, we rely on our briefs that we have filed. Your Honours, Mr. Sainovic and the other appellants' written submissions fundamentally fail to accept that this is an appellate proceeding, that this is not a de novo review hearing, that this is not a forum to re-argue positions advanced at trial. In order to unseat the Trial Chamber's factual conclusions, based on the assessment of the evidence, the appellants must demonstrate that the conclusions were ones that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have reached when assessing the totality of the evidence and that those findings occasioned a miscarriage of justice. This they fail to do. And Mr. Fila in his submissions constantly spoke of one little piece of evidence offered, an argument that he advanced at trial, pointed to other pieces of evidence, and said that the Trial Chamber got the factual assessment wrong, but throughout his submission he has ignored the fundamental facts that the Trial Chamber used in framing its assessment of the evidence, and that is the pattern of crimes starting on March 24th 1999 and continuing for a two-month period, during which time 700.000-plus Kosovo Albanians were displaced. It's in that context that the analysis takes place, not in isolation as to what happened at a meeting and what Mr. Sainovic did or said at a meeting. All of the events that led to the crimes and the proper inferences and conclusions to be drawn from those events in regard to the individual criminal responsibility of each of the appellants today. The Trial Chamber didn't conclude without having set out in its judgement how it went about its business of trying this very complex and lengthy trial. The Trial Chamber set out over 11 pages in Volume I, pages 17 to 27, exactly how it approached the assessment of the evidence and applied that approach consistently throughout the judgement. The Trial Chamber had the advantage of seeing and hearing the witnesses testify in court, had the advantage of assessing their demeanour, and had the advantage of forming an impression as to their credibility. And Mr. Fila argues that that should all be rejected. But because another witness said something else, the Trial Chamber's conclusion, in light of the totality of the evidence, should simply be ignored and another finding replace it and the finding beyond a reasonable doubt disturbed. The Trial Chamber carefully sifted and weighed the evidence and gave reasons for its treatment of controversial evidence. Where there was doubt, the Trial Chamber gave that doubt or the benefit of the doubt to the accused. Where the Trial Chamber rejected evidence or assertions made by the parties, it gave reasons. The Trial Chamber's findings, we would submit, are entitled to a significant margin of deference. Throughout the trial judgement's over 1300 pages in three main volumes, its factual findings are supported by detailed references to evidence on the record. Where it based conclusions on circumstantial evidence, it did so mindful that the conclusion must be the only reasonable conclusion on the totality of the evidence. At Volume I, paragraph 39, the Trial Chamber specifically referred to the Delalic appeal judgement, paragraph 458, which defined a circumstantial case: "A circumstantial case consists of evidence of a number of different circumstances which, taken in combination, point to the guilt of the accused person because they would usually exist in combination only because the accused did what is alleged against him ..." The Defence submission today suggests that you look at individual pieces of evidence, not all of it in combination. And what is significant to the analysis of this judgement is that the Trial Chamber correctly understood that when evaluating a circumstantial case it is the conclusion pointing to guilt which must be the only reasonable inference. It is not necessary, nor correct, to assess whether each individual strand of evidence can lead only to a finding of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. What is required is to consider all of the relevant findings based on the totality of relevant evidence before applying the beyond reasonable doubt standard to the essential elements required for conviction. Mr. Sainovic's submissions ask the Appeals Chamber to read the trial judgement piecemeal. However, the intricate links between the sections and the volumes of the judgement cannot be understood properly this way. A complete understanding comes only from a holistic reading of the entire judgement. Let me illustrate using the Trial Chamber's joint criminal enterprise findings. The core findings relating to the overall pattern of crimes found in Volume II, paragraphs 1150 to 1178, are referred to at Volume III, paragraph 46, and are integral to the conclusions about the crimes occurring according to a common purpose and thus to the existence of a joint criminal enterprise. The Trial Chamber focused primarily on the scale and pattern of displacement crimes in 1999, discussed throughout Volume II, to find a joint criminal enterprise was in existence at the time those crimes were committed. The Trial Chamber said so at Volume III, paragraph 17: "In the Chamber's view, the most compelling evidence of a common plan, design, or purpose is that which pertains to the pattern of crimes in 1999." In its findings at Volume III, paragraphs 89 to 96, having assessed all of the relevant evidence, not limited to the pattern of crimes but including a number of other factors, the Trial Chamber concluded the existence of a joint criminal enterprise was proven beyond a reasonable doubt. And in doing so, we submit, it was entitled to support its conclusions with evidence of events prior to the commission of crimes and the evidence of the concealment of over 700 bodies after. Your Honours, I will outline for you the -- in greater detail in a moment the -- why the Trial Chamber reasonably took into account the systematic pattern of crimes that took place at the hands of the VJ and MUP forces under the cover of the NATO bombing, demonstrate how this and numerous other factors supported the existence of a joint criminal enterprise. The Trial Chamber in its judgement determined, having regard to all of the evidence, that a co-ordinating mechanism between the MUP and VJ forces and Belgrade was integral to the commission of these crimes. The Joint Command, under the leadership of Sainovic and with the membership of Pavkovic and Lukic, was a crucial part of this co-ordinating mechanism. As Judge Liu noted at the beginning of this hearing, the Appeals Chamber's task is to examine errors of fact and law and is not to review every aspect of the Trial Chamber's reasoning and determine whether it agrees. We urge the Appeals Chamber in this case to rigorously apply the standard of review as an Appeals Chamber, to leave the evaluation and assessment of evidence to the Trial Chamber, it was its job, and point out that the Trial Judges in this case evaluated and assessed the evidence well, diligently, and cautiously and reasonably. And when you apply the standard of review properly and consistent with long-standing Appeals Chamber practice, we submit that your conclusion will be that the Trial Chamber's conclusion is reasoned and reasonable. Mr. Sainovic argues today and in his brief that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that a joint criminal enterprise existed and that he was a member of it. First, membership of the joint criminal enterprise. The Trial Chamber found that the JCE members held the highest political, military, and police leadership positions within the FRY and Serbia. And for our purposes its members included Milosevic, the FRY president and supreme commander of the VJ; Sainovic, the FRY Deputy Prime Minister responsible for FRY foreign policy and international relations and political co-ordinator of the VJ and MUP in Kosovo; Pavkovic, the commander of the 3rd Army; and Lukic, the head of the MUP staff for Kosovo. As noted in Volume III, paragraphs 91 and 92, the JCE members treated the entire Kosovo Albanian population as enemies of the FRY and Serbia. Instead of solving the political problem in Kosovo through democratic means and addressing crimes by the KLA through the effective use of police and judicial resources, the JCE members committed widespread and systematic crimes against the Kosovo Albanian population in 1999. Slobodan Milosevic played a pivotal role in this joint criminal enterprise. His role and influence in the JCE provides relevant context given that Sainovic, as Milosevic's man in Kosovo, was the conduit for Milosevic's influence in Kosovo. And there are a series of findings confirming Milosevic's role. Milosevic wielded significant power during the indictment period, Volume I, paragraphs 291 and 467. Also, as found by the Trial Chamber at Volume I, paragraphs 284, 467, 485, and Volume III, 468, he was at the apex of the executive chain of command of the VJ throughout the conflict and had significant de facto powers over the MUP. The Chamber found at Volume I, paragraphs 1109 and 1111, that it was through Milosevic's de facto authority that the Joint Command for Kosovo was created to ensure greater co-ordination between MUP and VJ forces and to enable him to direct the actions of the MUP. Milosevic orchestrated the events in Kosovo through all of the accused and particularly Sainovic. For example, he issued orders to the MUP personnel in Kosovo, often through Sainovic as noted in Volume III, 274. Through Sainovic, Milosevic gave approval for the activities of the VJ and the MUP in Kosovo and issued his instructions accordingly. You will find that at Volume III, paragraph 331. And Milosevic also promoted Pavkovic and Ojdanic towards the end of 1998 to facilitate implementation of the common purpose as noted in Volume III, paragraph 85. The Trial Chamber found that all of the JCE members, including Sainovic, shared Milosevic's sentiments about Kosovo. It was through his relationship with Milosevic that Sainovic developed the influence and authority he needed to co-ordinate the activities in Kosovo. You will find these findings at Volume III, paragraphs 427, 462, 466, and 467. Your Honours, before addressing the challenges to the findings and evidence supporting the existence of the JCE, I will briefly discuss the formation of the common purpose of the joint criminal enterprise. In examining whether there was a common purpose, as I have indicated earlier, the Trial Chamber considered the pattern of crimes, the concealment of bodies, and a number of other factors which preceded the crimes in some cases by many months. The Trial Chamber's findings on these other matters confirmed that it accepted that the common purpose had crystallised no later than October 1998 as pled in paragraph 20 of the indictment. First, at Volume III, paragraphs 68 and 72, the Chamber found that the disarming of Kosovo Albanians and the arming of non-Albanians was "designed to render the Kosovo Albanian population vulnerable to the forces of the FRY and Serbia, while at the same time empowering the non-Albanian population." It is express in this finding that the efforts to arm and disarm which continued through October 1998 formed part of the common plan. At Volume III, paragraph 85, the Trial Chamber confirmed that the common plan continued to exist at the end of 1998. The Trial Chamber reasoned that Ojdanic's promotion on 24 November 1998 and Pavkovic's promotion on 28 December 1998 were done "intentionally ... by Milosevic, a member of the joint criminal enterprise, in order to facilitate the implementation of the common purpose." In Volume III, paragraph 778, the Trial Chamber added that Pavkovic's promotion was a reward "for his participation in the joint criminal enterprise." In this way, the Trial Chamber confirmed that the common purpose had been in existence well before December 1998. At Volume III, paragraphs 76 and 92, the Chamber confirmed that the common purpose was evident during the Rambouillet and Paris negotiations in February of 1999. FRY and Serbian forces "made use of the period of negotiations" to delay an international military presence in Kosovo and bring in additional forces in breach of the October Agreements in order for to be in position to mount the widespread attack in the spring. The Chamber noted that "these dynamic and intertwined processes are indicative of a common purpose." And finally, at Volume III, paragraph 92, the Chamber drew upon its earlier findings and concluded that the NATO bombing provided the JCE members with the "opportunity" to undertake the displacement campaign. It added that this was an opportunity for which the JCE members "had been waiting and for which they had prepared by moving additional forces into Kosovo and by the arming and disarming process." Although the Trial Chamber found at Volume III, paragraph 96, that the common purpose was at least in existence at the time of the indictment crimes starting on 24 March 1999, it in no way limited the existence of the common purpose to this period. Indeed, as its other findings demonstrate, the Trial Chamber clearly considered the common purpose to be in existence earlier and our submission is no later than October 1998. The conclusion that the common plan had crystallised well before the indictment crimes is consistent with the Trial Chamber's findings that the widespread and organised expulsions throughout Kosovo required the -- I'm sorry. That the indictment crimes is consistent with the Chamber's findings that the widespread and organised expulsions throughout Kosovo, the implementation of the common plan, required significant planning and co-ordination, and I refer you to Volume II, paragraphs 48 and 888. Now, turning to the Chamber's findings regarding the existence of a joint criminal enterprise. The Trial Chamber carefully considered a large and solid body of relevant evidence including the acts and conduct of the accused to find the existence of a joint criminal enterprise. As the Trial Chamber noted at Volume III, paragraph 17, the "most compelling evidence" of the existence of the common criminal purpose was the discernible pattern of numerous crimes in 1999, including the forcible displacement of the Kosovo Albanian population which was evident as early as 24 March. The crimes were highly co-ordinated, systematic, and premeditated. They were of such a nature, scale, and cruelty as to establish the foundation for the Chamber's findings of a joint criminal enterprise among the political, military, and police leadership in the FRY Serbia to forcibly displace the Kosovo Albanian population. And I refer you again to Volume III, paragraph 95. The implementation of this pattern of crimes across Kosovo in such a short time, some two months, required a high level of co-operation and co-ordination between the MUP, the VJ, and the highest political levels. And I refer you to Volume I, paragraphs 1023, 1041, 1054, 1123, and 1151; Volume II, paragraphs 48, 253, 888; and Volume III, paragraph 468, 819, and 1132. The implementation of the pattern of crimes was accomplished through a system of co-ordination carried out by the three JCE members who are appellants in these proceedings, Mr. Sainovic, General Pavkovic, and General Lukic, in particular through the Joint Command, a mechanism in which the Chamber found Sainovic played a central role and I will discuss that later. First, the crimes in brief. In the first three days of the campaign, the joint forces attacked virtually every major town in Kosovo, including Pristina, Prizren, Djakovica, Kosovska Mitrovica, and Pec. The VJ and MUP forces also systematically attacked smaller surrounding towns and villages in Kosovo. The Chamber found that over 27 towns and villages throughout Kosovo within -- and within the 13 representative municipalities charged in the indictment were attacked and had their Albanian population displaced. This is reflected in Volume II, paragraphs 1181 to 1262. It is noted at Volume II, paragraph 1150, as a result of these co-ordinated efforts, over 300.000 Kosovo Albanians were expelled by the end of the campaign's first week. By the end of the second week, April 5th, that number doubled to 613.530. And by 30 April, 715.158 Kosovo Albanians had been expelled. To put these numbers in context, in a little over two months, approximately half of the Kosovo Albanian population was expelled and forced into Albania, Macedonia, and Montenegro. Moving now to the pattern of crimes. The Chamber found that the VJ and the MUP units acted with a high degree of co-ordination in expelling the Kosovo Albanian population, Volume I, paragraphs 1033 to 1043. Months in advance of the attacks, FRY and Serbian forces began to make preparations which laid the groundwork for the mass expulsions. For instance, in 1998 and early 1999, non-Albanians in Pristina were secretly armed by the VJ and the MUP. Simultaneously, the VJ and the MUP forces disarmed Kosovo Albanians in the town; that's found in Volume III, paragraphs 52, 54, 62, and 72. In the weeks preceding the NATO attacks, MUP, VJ, and Serb paramilitary forces were reinforced in and around Pristina despite the absence of significant KLA presence in the area, Volume II , paragraphs 808, 811 to 813. With this preparatory work in place, on 24 March 1999 and under the cover of the NATO campaign, VJ and MUP forces launched a co-ordinated wave of violence and terror throughout Kosovo intended to expel the Albanian population, found in Volume III, paragraphs 41 and 46. In some cases, such as the villages and towns of Pec, Pristina, Vladovo, and Sojevo, the joint forces would go door to door, forcibly expelling Albanians from their homes, Volume II, paragraph 48 for Pec; paragraph 885 for Pristina; 1247 for Zegra and Vladovo; 1250 for Sojevo, just as examples. In other cases, such as in Celina, Staro Selo, and Dubrava, the joint forces deliberately created a climate of fear intended to drive out the Albanians, Volume II, paragraph 311 for Celina; 885 for -- I'm sorry, 1251 for Staro Selo and 1247 for Vladovo. The VJ forces would often first surround the town or village and begin shelling the area. The VJ and MUP forces then, individually or together, would enter the town, terrorise the villagers through murder, threats of death, looting, the burning of homes or the brandishing of weapons, Volume II, paragraph 1060 to 1061 and -- I'm sorry, 1160 to 1161 and 1164. Kosovo Albanian residents often received an ultimatum, either to abandon their homes or to be killed. Your Honours can see that at Volume II, paragraphs 230, 718, and 839 in relation to the crimes committed in Reka/Caragoj Valley, Suva Reka, Zabare, and Pristina. As a result of these co-ordinated attacks by the VJ and the MUP, Kosovo Albanians were forced from their homes, funneled into massive convoys, and forced to the borders of Albania, Montenegro, and Macedonia. In some instances, Kosovo Albanian houses were occupied by Serbs. For instance, as noted in Volume II, paragraphs 831 to 832, in Pristina, many of the houses belonging to Kosovo Albanians were then occupied by the VJ and the MUP themselves and used to house official organs of the FRY and Serbian government. VJ and MUP forces often controlled the convoys by blocking roads and passages and ensuring that the Kosovo Albanians were directed to the border and could not take refuge in Kosovo. The convoys of Kosovo Albanians were sometimes led at gunpoint. Other times the VJ/MUP forces would direct the convoys to transportation depots where trains, buses, and trucks were assembled. I refer you to Volume II, paragraph 334 for Celine and 1167 for Pristina. The Kosovo Albanians were forced onto trains or vehicles which were severely overcrowded and transported to the different border crossings. Groups of refugees formed at these transportation depots until the Kosovo Albanians were expelled. As the convoys proceeded to the borders, the Kosovo Albanians continued to be subjected to further abuse and threats. Convoys departing from Pristina, for example, were subject to VJ and MUP insults. The VJ and MUP would curse and shout, "Kosovo does not belong to you Albanians, it belongs to Serbs," "we're going to kill you Albanians." You can find that at Volume II, paragraph 859. At the different border points and before expelling the Kosovo Albanians, MUP and VJ forces seized and destroyed their identification documents, including passports, driver's licences, in order to make their return to Kosovo difficult, if not impossible. You find that at Volume III, paragraph 32. According to the Trial Chamber, the confiscation and destruction of identification documents was amongst the strongest indicators demonstrating the existence of the common criminal purpose, Volume III, paragraph 40. The confiscation was a common practice, according to the Trial Chamber, and I have too many references on that point to give you at this point. The Trial Chamber took into account evidence of declarations made by FRY/Serbian forces that Kosovo Albanians would not come back to Kosovo when confiscating these documents. Pavkovic himself acknowledged this practice by MUP members, which is found at Volume III, paragraphs 720 and 775. Former VJ officers also testified as to the existence of orders to confiscate ID documents, Volume III, paragraphs 34 and 39. For example, K89 , a VJ soldier in Djakovica, testified that his commanding officer specifically told him that: "... not a single Albanian ear was to remain in Kosovo and that their identification papers were to be torn, so as to prevent them from coming back." And that's found at transcript 9124, 9154, and 9201. It's quoted at Volume III, paragraph 34. The Trial Chamber properly rejected the evidence of MUP or VJ officials denying the existence of such a practice. The Trial Chamber was also entitled to find that both MUP and VJ officials were involved on the basis of witness testimony that implicated the VJ. The Chamber properly considered and rejected Mr. Sainovic's assertions that the confiscation and destruction of identification documents did not cause the Kosovo Albanians to lose citizenship, but it did find that it would be more difficult for forcibly expelled Kosovo Albanians to return to Kosovo without proof of identity or citizenship or to obtain new identification documents from the Serb or FRY/Serbian forces or authorities. The VJ and the MUP also committed other crimes against Kosovo Albanians during the campaign of forcible displacement, some of which the Chamber found to be joint criminal enterprise III crimes. These included the looting and destruction of homes or property belonging to Kosovo Albanians, the damage or destruction of cultural, historic, or religious buildings, such as mosques; the summary execution of Kosovo Albanian civilians and the sexual assault and rape of Kosovo Albanian women. Examples of that are found throughout Volume II. The pattern and scale of the MUP/VJ displacement crimes shows that they were not random or spontaneous. As found by the Trial Chamber, they were committed pursuant to the common criminal purpose. The crimes were designed, as noted in Volume II, paragraphs 1156 and 1178, to systematically terrorise the Kosovo Albanian population into leaving Kosovo and required a high level of co-ordination. The Chamber properly found that co-ordination became the responsibility of Sainovic, Pavkovic, and Lukic and was accomplished through the system put in place by Milosevic. But it wasn't just the pattern and scale of crimes that influenced the Chamber's decision. It was also the strength of the evidence showing the pattern. The Trial Chamber concluded that there was a discernible pattern of crimes after a detailed and careful analysis of over 400 pages, spanning almost the entirety of Volume II, running from paragraph 1 to paragraph 1149. The numerous Albanian witnesses who testified about their own experiences and that of their relatives, friends, and neighbours gave a consistent account of the broad pattern of violence and terror created and entertained by the FRY/Serbian forces. Sainovic's challenges of the Chamber's reliance on Kosovo Albanian witnesses by arguing their consistency between their evidence indicates that they are in-credible, which he made at trial and continues to make in his brief, was dealt with by the Trial Chamber reasonably and it came to a very reasoned opinion that the testimony of the Kosovo Albanians was reliable, noting that it was inconceivable that such detailed and consistent accounts of the events could be concocted. The Trial Chamber noted that the witnesses came from 13 different municipalities and generally had no connection to one another. It concluded that the accounts of the events by Kosovo Albanians were similar because they experienced and witnessed the same pattern of crimes methodically implemented by FRY/Serbian forces across Kosovo. The evidence of Kosovo Albanian witnesses was also corroborated by several witnesses who were members of the VJ or MUP at the time of these events and some of whom were involved in the crimes against Kosovo Albanians. For example, the testimony of K73, a former VJ member, is quoted at Volume II, paragraph 1172: "... all of us took part in that operation, found it, if I can say, unpleasant to expel women, children, elderly persons, and invalids. I know the KLA pretty well and I've not seen a single woman of 70 years old or a child or anybody in the KLA, people like that cannot be fighters or terrorists. Or people in wheelchairs. But we expelled them all from the baby in the cradle to the elderly people in wheelchairs and that's the problem I have today." Another VJ member, K90: "... explained that the orders his unit received to 'relocate' people were never written, but they were passed down verbally because the authorities had learned from experience in Croatia and Bosnia that such orders should not be in writing," "that orders that important would have to be approved at the highest levels as these actions could not be ordered by a local commander alone," and "that these orders were always only related to Kosovo Albanian villages." You will find that at Volume II, paragraph 153. And it's not that the evidence of Kosovo Albanian witnesses was not corroborated, that the Chamber was accepting their version, it was corroborated by expert and forensic evidence, by MUP and VJ documentation and video footage, and evidence from foreign journalists present in Kosovo during the crimes, such as Antonio Russo, an Italian journalist who was present in Pristina and was expelled with the Kosovo Albanians living there. I refer Your Honours to the findings set out in our response brief at paragraph 266 and the supporting footnotes on this -- on the corroboration point. In light of this strong and consistent body of evidence, the Trial Chamber was correct to dismiss witness evidence denying the existence of a plan to expel Kosovo Albanian civilians. The Chamber was also correct to consider and then reject alternative explanations for the mass expulsions. These conclusions and some of the Chamber's reasoning can be found in Volume II, paragraph 1175 to 1179. Contrary to Sainovic's submissions this morning, the Trial Chamber found that the NATO bombing did not cause displacement en masse of Kosovo Albanians. The Chamber noted the fact that none of the Kosovo Albanians who testified listed the NATO bombing as among the causes of their or others' departure. As the Chamber found, the NATO campaign was, in fact, an opportunity for the JCE members to implement the criminal purpose, allowing them to inflict a heavy blow to the KLA and forcibly displace enough Kosovo Albanian civilians to change the ethnic balance of Kosovo and blame "with plausible deniability" both the KLA and NATO, and that's found at Volume III, paragraph 92. The JCE members were found to have been waiting for such an opportunity. Their forces were at full strength in the days immediately prior to the NATO campaign which began on 24 March. The JCE members were fully prepared to take advantage of the moment when it arrived, having used the negotiations period and subsequent delay in the arrival of international military presence to send additional forces to Kosovo in breach of the October Agreements. I refer you to Volume III, paragraphs 76 and 92. The Trial Chamber considered and rejected other explanations for the expulsions. It rejected Defence allegations that the combat action between the KLA and FRY/Serbian forces could have been the primary cause of the displacements. That's at Volume II, paragraph 1177; Volume II, paragraphs 285, 887, and 1175. It considered and rejected the argument that the crimes were a legitimate response to KLA action by noting comparatively small numbers of KLA members and their lack of fighting equipment, Volume II, paragraph 1177, and the heavy-handed manner in which the VJ and MUP fought the KLA, including their use of indiscriminate violence against civilian people and property. That's paragraph 1178, Volume II. Finally, the Trial Chamber found that in two locations the departure of Kosovo Albanians did occur in part due to KLA instructions. However, it found that this did not undermine its conclusion that Kosovo Albanian civilians left en masse because of the violent actions of the FRY/Serbian forces in light of the strength of the evidence presented in the case and I refer you to Volume II, 1175. Apart from the Chamber's findings of the widespread, organised, and co-ordinated campaign of violence and fear, the Chamber also determined that the JCE existed based on other factors, such as the preparatory acts taken in the months leading up to the crimes and the clandestine operations in April and May 1999 to conceal 700 bodies through their exhumation, transportation, and reburial in Serbia proper. I have discussed many of these preparatory acts already in discussing the formulation of the common plan. They are fully detailed in Volume III, paragraphs 48 to 96. Taking into account this wealth of mutually reinforcing evidence, none of the appellant's piecemeal attacks, taken individually or collectively, undermine the reasonableness of the Trial Chamber's finding that a joint criminal enterprise existed. Now, let me turn just very briefly to Joint Command. The common criminal purpose was carried out by the JCE members through a system of co-ordination which in 1999 had manifested itself as an organisation called the Joint Command and the Chamber's conclusion that a system of co-ordination similar to the Joint Command was active in 1999 was reasonable because a massive attack that was carried out under the cover of NATO bombings could not happen spontaneously. It required planning, it required co-ordination, and it required it at the highest levels; highest levels of the police, highest levels of the military, and highest political levels. And, indeed, the Trial Chamber found a high level of co-ordination and co-operation between the VJ and the MUP existed during the planning and execution of the joint operations commencing in March 1999, Volume I, paragraph 1023. Mr. Sainovic challenges the Trial Chamber's findings that a body called the Joint Command existed after October 1998 and throughout 1999, and that this body had the power to command forces on the ground and that Sainovic was ever a part of it. Similar arguments are advanced by Pavkovic, Lukic, and Lazarevic. And these will be addressed by my colleagues later in the week. Ms. Martin Salgado will deal in more detail with Mr. Sainovic's personal contributions, and I'll just focus on the existence and authority of the Joint Command. The challenges seek to undermine the Chamber's core findings that the Joint Command "played a significant role in directing and co-ordinating the activities of the VJ and the MUP in Kosovo in both 1998 and 1999," Volume III, paragraph 1023, and that "in 1999 the co-ordination system continued to function," Volume I, paragraph 1151. These were reasonable conclusions to draw, given the extensive evidence upon which they were based, such as: Explicit Joint Command orders from 1999, a Joint Command meeting on 1 June 1999 mirroring the 1988 [sic] meetings; numerous references to the Joint Command throughout 1999; and other evidence which demonstrates that the Joint Command system continued to function in 1999 and co-ordinate the joint operations of the VJ and the MUP. While there is more evidence from 1998 detailing the inner workings of the Joint Command, for instance, minutes of an almost daily Joint Command meetings, the evidence nonetheless demonstrates that the need for this co-ordination continued into 1999 and did -- as did the co-ordination system including the Joint Command itself. The need for the Joint Command is demonstrated by the fact and the evidence that the VJ and the MUP could not work effectively together. If left to themselves, they wouldn't -- in fact would not. The Trial Chamber found that they tried in early 1998 and it did not work well, Volume I, paragraph 1025. As a result, in May or June 1998, efforts began to improve co-ordination under Milosevic's direction, ultimately resulting in the formation of the Joint Command body, Volume I, paragraphs 1005 to 1011 and 1109. Milosevic noted that when the system was first created in the second half of 1998, the police, the army, and politicians each had a part to play in the anti-terrorism plan that had been adopted. I refer you to Volume I, paragraph 995. The Trial Chamber found that when important actors, including the accused, referred to the Joint Command in 1999, they were adverting to this whole system of co-ordination, Volume I, paragraph 1151. The Joint Command comprised high-ranking members of the VJ and MUP and high-ranking civilian leaders like Milomir Minic, president of the Assembly and member of the Working Group for Kosovo, and of course Sainovic. Minic and Sainovic played a leadership role in 1998 and when Minic left Kosovo at the end of 1998, Sainovic remained to continue the co-ordination. The political dimension was also key for Milosevic. In 1999, Sainovic was the person Milosevic used to orchestrate the events in Kosovo. I refer you to Volume III, 467. And as one of Milosevic's closest advisors, he was the person to do the job. Several witnesses were of the view that Milosevic was in total control and Sainovic was the next in line, Volume III, paragraphs 200, 409, and 467. The Joint Command also allowed Slobodan Milosevic to direct the actions of the MUP in Kosovo, Volume I, paragraph 1110 and Volume III, 274. Through Sainovic, together with Pavkovic and Lukic, Milosevic could co-ordinate the activities of the MUP and the VJ. It enabled Milosevic to direct the MUP, a republican organ, which was otherwise outside the scope of his federal powers. It also allowed him to deploy VJ units in Kosovo despite objections within the VJ. Against this backdrop, I will explain why, and very briefly, I'm almost done, the Trial Chamber reasonably concluded that this system of co-ordination continued into 1999 and that this system had an important influence on the events on the ground. First, there are 16 orders from 1999 which all bear the heading "Joint Command," Volume I, paragraph 1122, containing orders for the engagement of units. At the end of each order there is some variant of the phrase "The Joint Command for KiM shall command and control all forces during combat operations from the area of Pristina," and the phrase "Joint Command" appears until the header and signature block, Volume I, paragraph 1122 and 1137. Significantly, the Trial Chamber noted that several of the 1999 Joint Command orders identify forces engaging in combat operations in areas and on dates that correspond to the crime sites in the indictment. I refer to Volume I, paragraph 1123, and Volume III, paragraph 695. For example, the order of the 549th Motorised Brigade from 23 March 1999 matches the general task and location specified in a Joint Command order also dated 23 March. Both orders target Suva Reka-Orahovac with the task of destroying Siptar forces. These orders correspond to the wave of attacks carried out in several towns in the Orahovac municipality, found at Volume II, paragraph 296. The after-action report by the 549th Motorised Brigade states the co-ordination of the forces functioned well and that the command of the forces was under the Joint Command of the MUP and VJ. The judgement gives further examples at Volume I, paragraphs 1124 to 1126. The Trial Chamber found that these orders originated from the Pristina Corps command and that the VJ and MUP chains of command remained intact throughout 1999. The system of co-ordination that operated in 1999 did not supplant the chains of command but utilised them through the influence of its members. The Trial Chamber found that in 1998 that while some Joint Command members might not have had the de jure powers to order MUP and VJ units, the individual members of the Joint Command brought their de facto influence to bear on how the plan for the suppression of terrorism in Kosovo was put into effect. I refer you to Volume I, paragraph 1110. Similarly, it found that the 1999 orders with the heading "Joint Command" lent a greater air of authority to the commands issued and that references to the Joint Command constituted an important factor during the planning and implementation of joint operations between the MUP and the VJ, Volume I, paragraph 1151.
