utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I left off just before the break explaining why the Trial Chamber reasonably concluded that the system of co-ordination continued into 1999 and that the system had an important influence on the events on the ground. The first discussion was in relation to the 16 orders under the title "Joint Command" issued in 1999. The second is the evidence of a meeting on 1 June 1999 that was similar to the Joint Command meetings held throughout 1998. Sainovic, Pavkovic, and Lukic were there. Presentations by Pavkovic and Lukic included very technical details about what was going on during VJ and MUP activities. General Vasiljevic, the former head of the VJ security administration, testified that everyone treated Sainovic deferentially throughout and that the reports focused only on that day's activities, giving him the impression that the meetings were a daily occurrence, and that's Volume I, paragraph 1145. This is consistent with the fact that in 1998, between July and October, there was evidence of almost daily meetings of the Joint Command. And that's Exhibit P1468. The third piece of evidence is the need for and continued existence of the Joint Command in 1999 was clear from another meeting held on 29 October 1988 -- or 1998. It was chaired by Milosevic and attended by Sainovic, Milutinovic, Pavkovic, and Lukic. I refer you to Volume I, paragraphs 1097 and 1099. And agreement was reached at that meeting that the Joint Command should continue. Milosevic pointed towards "the need for the continuing function of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija and the co-ordination staff." I apologise to my colleagues for the mispronunciation. Sainovic himself agreed by expressing support for the continuation of the Joint Command, and these quotations are cited by the Trial Chamber in Volume I, 1099. And fourth, the Trial Chamber cited several other independent pieces of evidence regarding the Joint Command's authority in 1999. Vasiljevic stated that the Joint Command in 1999 had the force of a mini-Supreme Command, Volume I, paragraph 1114. Ojdanic, Chief of the General Staff of the VJ, stated at a VJ General Staff collegium held on 21 January 1999 that if the "joint staff, command or whatever" decided that an operation in the Racak village could not be carried out without the VJ's assistance, they would need the approval of the FRY president; alternatively, the Joint Command might be receiving orders directly from the FRY president which they could pass on to him, Volume I, paragraph 1120. Pavkovic sent a letter on 25 May 1999 regarding the failed attempts at having the MUP resubordinate to the VJ. He stated that the order should be either reinforced or annulled. If annulled, command of the MUP should be returned to the hands of the Ministry of the Interior through the Joint Command as had so far been the case, and that's found in Volume I, paragraph 1121. And finally, in June 2001, Pavkovic made a statement on the VJ web site concerning the refrigerated lorry in the concealment of bodies that was found in the Danube in 1999. In relation to the incident he stated that police co-operation with the army "was co-ordinated through political actors in the Joint Command, formed for that purpose." That quotation is used by the Trial Chamber in Volume I, paragraph 1117. Against this backdrop of evidence from both 1998 and 1999, the Trial Chamber reasonably found that the Joint Command system of co-ordination continued to function in 1999 and facilitated the co-operation and co-ordination of the VJ and MUP. This co-operation and co-ordination was crucial to the successful implementation of the joint criminal enterprise and had direct impact on the events on the ground. I just will conclude my remarks and then pass the podium over to Ms. Martin Salgado, and I will answer the last question posed by Your Honours to the parties. And this deals with the crimes in Tusilje. We agree that Tusilje should have been pled in the indictment and that no corrective actions were taken in our pre-trial brief or 65 ter filings. The evidence led at trial and the Chamber's findings show that Tusilje was a collection point for Kosovo Albanians fleeing from the village of Turcevac and that accused were convicted of the deportations from Turcevac. On Friday we will discuss why even were the Chamber to overturn the Tusilje convictions there should be no impact on sentencing. The accused were still convicted of the deportation of over 700.000 Kosovo Albanians from the 13 representative municipalities. The gravity and scale of the crimes and their impact on the victims, as we will argue on Friday, warrant an increase in sentences regardless of the disposition of the Tusilje conviction. Unless you have questions of me specifically, I will pass the podium to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Tuzmukhamedov has a question to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Liu. Back in Arusha I went by Judge T. Mr. Kremer, you stated a few moments ago that JCE had an important influence on the events on the ground. And the statement echos the Trial Chamber's finding that the Joint Command had influence over the MUP and VJ in respect of the implementation of the various stages of the plan for combatting terrorism. How would you characterise in legal and in administrative terms the source and the extent of this influence and practice? In particular, how binding was this influence? What were the modes of its implementation? What would be the consequences of non-compliance? And could you refer to any instances of non-compliance? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: The influence stems from the influence of Slobodan Milosevic, who was the -- one of the JCE members and who had at that point in time substantial power over all events in the FRY and Serbia. The influence was exercised by being the point person for Milosevic on the ground. And to the extent that there was disagreement with the issues, Milosevic could replace individuals, as he did with General Perisic who was replaced with Samardzic. Samardzic was replaced by General Pavkovic at the end of 1998. The ultimate discussions in relation to some of these issues moved and there's evidence of meetings in Belgrade where Pavkovic and Lukic give reports to Milosevic and Sainovic is present. And so the influence and authority of Sainovic exists throughout as the representative and is evident both in meetings in Belgrade and is evident in his being placed in the position in charge of the KVM and also his going to MUP meetings, his going to VJ meetings, and demonstrating his influence. It wasn't sort of a - what am I saying? The meetings themselves weren't used to exercise the influence; the influence was palpable through their ability of all three of the joint criminal enterprises to bring to bear their influences to make the joint co-operation work. To the extent that trains had to be rescheduled, to the extent that buses had to be available, to the extent that civilian authorities had to be co-operating as well, everything was consolidated so that the events could take place starting when the NATO bombings started, to seize that opportunity and set free all of the resources that had been put in place all over Kosovo in order to carry out the common criminal purpose. Bringing in extra military personnel, bringing in extra police personnel, ensuring that the police and the military worked together at the same places and accomplishing the political ends because the notional goal was to combat terrorism, to fight the KLA. But in practice - as the Chamber found - what was really happening on the ground in a consolidated and co-ordinated way was that the inhabitants of Kosovo who were Albanian were being pushed out in order to change the balance of the population to give the Serbs a majority or aiming towards a majority and to do it by criminal means. Because all over Kosovo in the 13 municipalities the criminal means were demonstrated visibly and over and over and over again in the first several weeks of the campaign.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Actually, I didn't ask you about Mr. Sainovic personally, but thank you for that anyway. I don't want to be annoying, but I think that my question was very specific as to the description in legal and in administrative terms the sources of the influence of the Joint Command on events on the ground and about specific instances, if you could think of any, of consequences of non-compliance with the manifestations of that influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: The Joint Command operated as a co-ordinating body, so there are no specific legal authorities that it possessed. The VJ chain of command operated and the MUP chain of command operated. The VJ chain of command went up to the supreme commander, Milosevic; the MUP chain of command went to the minister of interior. But getting them to work together, there was no legal vehicle that was -- presently it was done through the strong will and political influence of Slobodan Milosevic, through his agent, Mr. Sainovic. To the extent that there is no example of someone refusing to follow ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: There are examples in Volume I of Pavkovic disagreeing with the 3rd Army when he's head of the Pristina Corps command, but it's within the same chain of command as opposed to refusing to follow a Joint Command order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Kremer, I have a question to ask you. What is your position on the relationship between the common criminal purpose in 1998 and the joint criminal enterprise in 1999? This morning the Defence counsel submitted that even if there is joint criminal enterprise, the Trial Chamber should have to look into the evidence in 1999 instead of 1998. What's your position on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: The simple answer, Your Honour, is that the Trial Chamber looked at events prior to the commission of the crimes. Let's start on March 24th, 1999, and look back to confirm and support its findings that there was at least a joint criminal enterprise on that date. And as they looked back, looking at the preparations for the attacks on the Kosovo Albanians, starting March 24th, 1999, they found that the joint criminal enterprise was formed well before that. And when I spoke about the date of at least October this morning, I gave you examples of references that the Trial Chamber used to identify the fact that the joint criminal enterprise predated significantly the commencement date of the crimes. In terms of looking at 1998, I think the words of the Trial Chamber are clear. They're not looking at 1998 to confirm that there is a joint criminal enterprise, but to support their -- or they're using it to support their finding that there was a joint criminal enterprise evident from the events that took place on the ground, the pattern of the crimes, the widespread nature of the crimes that could only have occurred with the support, influence, and involvement of the senior military police and political leadership and then in order to evaluate that they go back and look at events that have similar factual relationships to the events that took place in 1999 and that dealt with those at length in terms of its analysis to ensure that the conclusion it was drawing on the existence of a joint criminal enterprise in 1999 were sound and reasonable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you. MS. MARTIN SALGADO: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I will be addressing the legal position in answer to Your Honours' tenth question at page 3 of the order for the preparation of the appeal hearing. I will also deal with the actus reus part of the question as it relates to Sainovic. My colleague, Ms. Monchy, will then address the mens rea part of that question as it relates to Sainovic and the remaining mens rea questions. The tenth question is as follows: "Discuss, as a legal matter as well as with respect to the particular Trial Chamber's findings for each appellant convicted of JCE I, whether the actus reus and mens rea of a JCE member may be fulfilled prior to the existence of the common purpose of the JCE." Before answering Your Honours' question on the law, I would simply like to clarify the terms used. When referring in the question to the "actus reus" "of a JCE member," we understand Your Honours to be asking after one specific objective element, namely, the participation of the accused in the common purpose. Participation in a common purpose requires conduct amounting to a significant contribution to further the common purpose. When referring to the "mens rea" "of a JCE member," we understand Your Honours to be asking after the two subjective elements of, for our purposes, the first category of joint criminal enterprise. And these are that: One, the accused intended the commission of the crime; and two, that the accused intended to participate in a common purpose aimed at the crime's commission. To answer your question then, as a matter of law, generally, an accused's actus reus - in the sense of his significant contribution - and his mens rea cannot be fulfilled prior to the existence of the common purpose. And the reasons for this position are as follows: The criminal purpose needs to be common to all of the persons acting together within a joint criminal enterprise, and this is the same as saying that they need to have a shared intent. Since an accused's contribution must significantly further the common purpose, in the sense that it must be in some way directed to the furthering of the common purpose, it cannot be fulfilled before that common purpose comes into existence. And similarly, the accused's mens rea cannot be fulfilled until it is shared by one or more members of the joint criminal enterprise. And we note in connection with this position that, where necessary, an accused may be held liable for conduct carried out before the existence of a common purpose under other modes of liability in the Statute. Now, the position just explained does not mean that the conduct carried out by an accused before the existence of the common purpose is irrelevant to his joint criminal enterprise liability. It can be relevant in at least two ways. First, it is clear that the state of mind and conduct of an accused prior to the existence of the common purpose can be taken into consideration as evidence of that accused's JCE mens rea, and our authority for this is Krajisnik appeals judgement paragraphs 200 to 204, paragraph 492, and also Krajisnik trial judgement, paragraphs 925 to 929. Second, an accused can bring in or make use of the results of conduct predating the existence of the common purpose to further that common purpose. "Bringing in" or "making use" of those results may then constitute a contribution to this common purpose, provided that: One, this "bringing in" or "making use of" is carried out with the required intent; and two, it significantly furthers the common purpose. And in such cases, it makes no sense to speak about "pre-JCE contributions," since it is the "bringing in" or "making use" of the results of previous conduct that amount to the contribution and this is done once the common purpose is in existence. And to give examples, other cases before this Tribunal have adopted this approach. So, for example, in Krajisnik, the Appeals Chamber affirmed the Trial Chamber's reliance on Krajisnik setting up of political structures before the period of the JCE's existence, which were later used to implement the common purpose during the JCE period. And you can find this at the Krajisnik appeals judgement, paragraphs 162 to 218. And similarly, in considering Martic's participation in the joint criminal enterprise, the Trial Chamber found that Martic's contacts with other JCE members before the common purpose, which then continued and intensified during the JCE period, resulted in substantial logistical and military support that was later used to further the common purpose. And our authority for that is at Martic appeal judgement, paragraph 117 and Martic trial judgement, paragraphs 445 and 448. Now, that is the position on the law, and we will separately address the findings for each appellant convicted under joint criminal enterprise liability. But for all of them, Your Honours, we submit that on the facts of this case, this issue does not arise. These appellants made their significant contribution to the common purpose and had the required intent during the time of the existence of the common purpose, which was well before the crimes were committed in 1999, and, at a minimum, throughout the period of the crimes charged. And that concludes my presentation on the legal part. As for the factual part of the question relating to Sainovic, we understand Your Honours to be asking: Was Sainovic found to have contributed to the joint criminal enterprise before the existence of the common purpose? And the short answer is no. As a member of the Joint Command and as the highest-ranking politician meeting with Pavkovic and Lukic, Sainovic continuously influenced and co-ordinated the activities of the forces of the FRY and Serbia in Kosovo. While Sainovic's significant contribution is grounded on conduct carried out throughout the period when the crimes were committed in 1999, his authority and involvement in Kosovo remained the same from the summer of 1998 onwards. And as such, his authority and involvement extended from then and into the crimes' period. And I intend to elaborate on this answer by explaining how Sainovic contributed to the common purpose and why his contribution was significant, and I'll do that by describing his role in 1998 and 1999. Turning, therefore, to his role in Kosovo. Sainovic was the political co-ordinator of the activities of the VJ and the MUP in Kosovo from the second half of 1998 to the beginning of the second half of 1999, and the authority for this is at Volume III, paragraphs 331 and 462. And I'll explain what is meant by "political co-ordinator." As Milosevic's man in Kosovo, Sainovic brought the political authority necessary to overcome the reluctance of the VJ and the MUP to work together in Kosovo. In addition, Sainovic gave Milosevic's approval for the actions of the VJ and the MUP and conveyed Milosevic's instructions and his own to those forces. And in this way, by bringing Pavkovic and Lukic together and giving them instructions, Sainovic co-ordinated and influenced the activities of the VJ and the MUP respectively. And these activities were then implemented by Pavkovic and Lukic down the MUP and VJ -- or down the VJ and MUP chains of command. Now, the Chamber reasonably found that Sainovic's involvement continued into the period when the crimes were committed in 1999. And that his authority at that time was undiminished and that the following factors did not change indicates the continuation of Sainovic's involvement and authority. First, the way he operated and his interlocutors were the same. In 1999, Sainovic continued to co-ordinate the forces in a manner similar to 1998. He had the help of the same people - that's Pavkovic and Lukic - with whom he was in continuous contact and he acted at the instigation of Milosevic. And that's at Volume III, paragraph 464. The second factor is that the de facto source of Sainovic's authority was also the same. He was one of the closest and most trusted associates of Milosevic both in 1998 and 1999. And thanks to this relationship, he led Joint Command meetings and other meetings with VJ and MUP officials. And also thanks to this relationship, he became chairman for the commission of co-operation with the KVM. And that's at Volume III, paragraph 427. And indeed while between November 1998 and March 1999, Milosevic was replacing individuals such as Perisic, Samardzic, and Dimitrijevic, he kept Sainovic in prominent roles dealing with Kosovo and this allowed Sainovic to expand his role as Milosevic's political representative in the province. And that is at Volume III, paragraph 427. The third factor, Your Honours, is that in 1999 Sainovic continued to show a deep familiarity with the events taking place in Kosovo and still travelled there often. And in fact, the bulk of his trips took place in late March and early April, when the majority of the crimes were committed. Turning to Sainovic's participation when the crimes were committed. Specifically during the crimes' period, Sainovic co-ordinated and influenced the activities of the VJ and the MUP in Kosovo, as a member of the Joint Command and as the highest-ranking politician meeting with Pavkovic and Lukic. Widespread crimes were committed through the activities which Sainovic co-ordinated, and in particular the joint VJ and MUP operations. Now, throughout the crimes period Sainovic was a member of the MUP -- of the Joint Command, I'm sorry, and the failure of the MUP to resubordinate to the VJ despite orders for it to do so in April 1999 confirms that there was a continued need for political involvement in co-ordinating these forces. And indeed, referring to problems of resubordination in May 1999, Vasiljevic gave evidence that "the executive command was in the hands of Mr. Sainovic down there, who was there for that purpose, to co-ordinate the activities of the army and the MUP." And that's at Volume III, paragraph 339. The 16 Joint Command orders in evidence, which Mr. Kremer mentioned this morning, are the product of the political co-ordination of joint VJ-MUP operations, some of which correspond to indictment crimes committed by VJ and/or MUP forces. The earliest Joint Command order in evidence from 1999 is dated 19th of March and it denotes Joint Command involvement just prior to when the crimes were committed, preparing the groundwork for the mass expulsions that soon followed. In addition to his Joint Command position in 1999, Sainovic's participation at meetings with VJ and MUP officials dealing with Kosovo further demonstrates that he was influencing and co-ordinating the VJ and the MUP during the crimes' period --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, counsel, would you please slow down for the sake of the translation. MS. MARTIN SALGADO: I apologise, Your Honour. In these meetings, Sainovic's role was to liaise between the VJ and the MUP and Milosevic. At meetings with the MUP leadership in Kosovo, Sainovic was ensuring co-ordination between the VJ and the MUP and was authorising MUP actions. He was also giving instructions and relaying Milosevic's orders. And he was doing this, despite the fact that he and Milosevic were federal politicians and therefore were not in the chain of command or in the formal chain of command of the republican MUP. And, for example, at the meeting of 4 April 1999 with senior police officials in Kosovo, which took place in Pristina, Sainovic declared the end of the first stage of anti-terrorist operations. In that same meeting, he also assigned two other very specific tasks, which, he said, were to be planned and carried out together with the VJ. And that's at Volume III, paragraph 341. At the MUP staff meeting of 7 May 1999, also in Pristina, Sainovic outlined the main objectives and tasks and said that after Operation Jezerce, and I apologise for the pronunciation, special police forces in co-operation with the VJ would "work on destroying the remaining terrorist groups." And at this same meeting -- I'm sorry, and that's from Volume III, paragraph 346. And at this same meeting he also referred to an order from Milosevic, stating that it should be communicated to all police commanders, as a task assigned by the Supreme Command. And contrary to the Defence argument of this morning, this shows Sainovic actually putting political weight behind the order and its communication. These meetings confirm Vasiljevic's evidence that in 1999 Sainovic was "to be informed and co-ordinate the eventual problems between the VJ and the MUP and to follow the overall situation on Kosovo, keeping Belgrade informed thereof." And that's at Volume III, paragraph 357. And reinforcing Sainovic's liaison function is the evidence that in June 1999 Ojdanic complained to Vasiljevic that Pavkovic was giving more importance to keeping Sainovic informed than to informing Ojdanic, his own immediate superior. And that's at Volume III, paragraph 361. Sainovic's pivotal role in co-ordinating MUP and VJ activities remained the same until the end of the 1999 campaign, and this is shown in the 1 June 1999 Joint Command meeting in Pristina attended by Sainovic, Lukic, Pavkovic, Lazarevic, and other VJ, MUP, and civilian leaders. At the 1 June 1999 meeting, Sainovic did a number of things: One, after detailed presentations by Pavkovic, Lazarevic, and Lukic on the day's VJ and MUP activities, Sainovic authorised their actions. He said, "Okay, do as you've planned," referring to an action in Drenica to engage 300 police officers, and that's at Volume III, paragraph 356. Two, he gave Milosevic's instructions and his own, and he did so by ordering that activities of the joint forces stop due to the agreement between Milosevic and Martti Ahtisaari, and when those at the meeting protested, exercised discretion by instructing completion of these activities in the following days. And that's at Volume III, paragraph 359, and indeed hostilities stopped on 10 June 1999, and that's at Volume III, paragraph 743. And we have heard this morning the argument that Sainovic could not have issued this order because, according to the Defence, the Military Technical Agreement had not been concluded. But it is clear from the testimony of Branko Krga, which is cited in Volume I, footnote 3322, that the agreement Sainovic was referring to was an interim agreement. And it is also clear from the testimony of Stojanovic, which is cited at Volume III, paragraph 356, that what Sainovic conveyed was that an agreement between the FRY and the international community would be signed soon, that it envisaged the withdrawal of the VJ and the MUP from Kosovo, and that this withdrawal would have to commence soon. As to its significance, Your Honours, Sainovic's conduct amounted to a significant contribution to the joint criminal enterprise because the organised campaign of forcible displacement implemented in 1999 entailed extensive co-operation and co-ordination between the VJ and the MUP in furtherance of the policy pursued by Belgrade. Moving on very briefly, Your Honours, to Sainovic's participation before the crimes' period. In addition to the specific evidence of his co-ordination and influence during the crimes, the Chamber relied on evidence of Sainovic's authority and involvement before this period. It correctly found on the basis of all of this evidence that he was the political co-ordinator of the VJ and the MUP throughout and that in this role he significantly contributed to the common purpose. And that's at 462 and 467. In the same way as during the NATO campaign, Sainovic co-ordinated and influenced the VJ and MUP in Kosovo in 1998 and before 24 March in 1999. The Chamber found that in 1998 he was one of the leading members of the Joint Command, and that as such he possessed extensive de facto powers over both the VJ and the MUP in Kosovo and, together with Pavkovic and Lukic, co-ordinated VJ and MUP activities in implementing the plan for combatting terrorism. And that's at Volume I, paragraph 1110; and Volume III, paragraphs 462, 468. Following the completion of this plan in October 1998, he co-ordinated the forces in Kosovo while chairman of the commission for co-operation with the KVM, and he did so by continuing to deal with and have influence over Pavkovic and Lukic without interruption, much like he had done before and much like he would continue doing after. And on this subject, let me just remark that Ojdanic's complaint that I have mentioned before, the one where in 1999 he says that Pavkovic is placing more importance of keeping Sainovic informed rather than on informing his immediate superior, this complaint actually reflects instructions that Sainovic had issued much before. There is evidence that on 12th November 1998, after assuming his role as chairman of the commission, Sainovic instructed Pavkovic and Lukic to continue with the already established practice of informing Sainovic of important incidents first and only then informing their own superiors. And that's at Volume III, paragraph 373. And as an example of this, the Chamber found that the way Sainovic managed the aftermath of the Podujevo and Racak incidents, which took place at the end of December 1998 and in mid-January 1999, respectively, demonstrated that he was in regular contact with Lukic and Pavkovic, exerted influence over them, and knew about impending joint VJ-MUP actions, and that's at Volume III, paragraphs 395, 401. To conclude, Your Honours, the Chamber reasonably found that Sainovic was one of the most crucial members of the joint criminal enterprise. In the months leading up to the crimes, Sainovic co-ordinated and influenced actions of the VJ and the MUP in Kosovo and acted as the liaison between these forces and Milosevic. Once the crimes began, Sainovic's continued co-ordination and influence significantly furthered the common purpose. And for that we ask that you see Volume III, paragraphs 462 and 467. And thus, in answer to Your Honours' tenth question, Sainovic's contribution to the joint criminal enterprise took place during the existence of the common purpose. And in response to Sainovic's appeal and his submissions here today, it is our position that his grounds of appeal relating to his contribution to the joint criminal enterprise should be dismissed. And unless Your Honours have any questions, I'll pass on to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Judge T. I'll go by Arusha way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: "Xiexie." Ms. Salgado, I'd like to address this term "political co-ordinator." I understand that this was the deduction of the Trial Chamber. Based on the evidence that they had, they concluded -- they "assigned" this role to Mr. Sainovic. In your response brief, you gave an interpretation of that conclusion of the Trial Chamber by stating that the term "political co-ordinator" was descriptive in nature. I have a feeling that during your presentation right now you went a little bit further than that, stating that this was a descriptive term. However, I guess my question is: Assuming there is a finding that the term "political co-ordinator" was not just a mere descriptive term, then how this could affect Mr. Sainovic's criminal responsibility? I have another question, but probably we should go step by step. MS. MARTIN SALGADO: Thank you, Your Honour. I certainly did not intend to depart in my submissions from our position in the brief, which is that the term "political co-ordinator" is descriptive. And it is used descriptively to, yes, give a label, so to speak to what, in our submission, is the contribution that he made, which is the co-ordinating and influencing the activities of the VJ and the MUP. And in our position, the term "political co-ordinator" condenses that significance essentially. As to the second part of your question -- I'm sorry. I believe it goes back to my first answer which is: What is important is that he made a contribution to the common purpose and that that contribution was significant. And we have described what that contribution is, which is co-ordinating and influencing. And as a result, I don't think that a finding on whether the term "political co-ordinator" is anything more than a descriptive term would have any effect on his criminal responsibility. And I hope I have understood Your Honours correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And the second one, by -- in fact, by quoting the Trial Chamber when you stated that Mr. Sainovic was the closest and most trusted associate of the late Mr. Milosevic, I think you came very close to another description of relationship between Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Milosevic. And the Trial Chamber stated that this was a special relationship, an assumption which was denied this morning by your friends across the aisle. But the Trial Chamber stated that this special relationship resulted to -- resulted in Sainovic undertaking a leading role during the Joint Command meetings. Could you elaborate on the characteristics of that close and most trusted relationship or special relationship - to use the terminology of the Trial Chamber? Was there anything out of the ordinary in that relationship? And what bearing the finding of the existence of that special relationship could have on Mr. Sainovic's criminal responsibility? MS. MARTIN SALGADO: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll begin with the second part of your question so as not -- again, the importance of his close relationship with Slobodan Milosevic is, in our view, two-fold. In the first place it goes towards describing his contribution to the common criminal purpose, and that is because, as I said, his contribution is co-ordinating and influencing the VJ and the MUP. And one of the ways he co-ordinates is by also acting as a liaison not just between the VJ and the MUP, but between the VJ, MUP, and Milosevic so that the common criminal purpose can be implemented through the forces in the ground but in furtherance of the policy pursued by Belgrade. So in that sense, his close relationship is -- evidences what his significant contribution is, which is that part of liaising between Milosevic and the forces in the ground. His close relationship also serves the role of showing the extent to which he had authority, the authority to, as we say, influence the activities of the VJ and the MUP in the ground. So it's also explanatory of why we say he was in a position to do the things he did in contribution to the common criminal purpose. And I'm verifying whether I've answered all of your questions, Your Honour. And, Your Honour, if I could rely on the judgement in Volume II in the section it devotes to his relationship with Milosevic for a more fuller -- or for a fuller description of what that relation amounted to. I hope this answers Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TUZMUKHAMEDOV
utterances.text: Thank you. MS. MARTIN SALGADO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, counsel, before you start I have to remind you that you only have six minutes to finish your response.

utterances.speaker: MS. MONCHY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I will try to meet the challenge and I will just focus on responding strictly to your questions relating to mens rea. Your Honours, regarding the first -- the remaining part of your tenth question which was just addressed by Ms. Martin Salgado, our response is quite short and straightforward. The Trial Chamber did not find that Sainovic had the shared intent for the JCE before the common purpose came into existence. Rather, the Trial Chamber properly took into account evidence from before, during, and after the commission of the crimes to find that Sainovic had the requisite intent at all times he contributed to the JCE. Turning now to your question number 11 relating to the relevance of Sainovic's knowledge of crimes in 1998. Well, Your Honours, the Trial Chamber reasonably relied upon Sainovic's knowledge that the use of excessive and disproportionate force by FRY and Serbian forces led to forcible displacements as one of the factors to infer Sainovic's mens rea. This is because this knowledge was a clear warning to Sainovic that the FRY and Serbian forces would behave in a similar way a few months later and again cause massive forcible displacement. Even if the crimes in 1998 were committed on a lower and less systematic scale than during the NATO campaign, Sainovic was on notice of the continuing risk of crimes by these forces. His knowledge was also relevant because Sainovic could be confident that by using those same forces to carry out a widespread and systematic campaign of terror and violence which involved destruction of private property, intimidation, and violence against Kosovo Albanians as in 1998, these forces would successfully achieve mass displacements in 1999. Finally, my third and last point on this issue, this is also relevant to show the pattern of Sainovic's conduct. Sainovic knew that the FRY and Serbian forces committed crimes in 1998, but he did nothing to change it. And instead, he continued co-ordinating these forces and supported their heavy-handed approach, and this is Volume III, paragraph 463. And he behaved in the exact same way during the NATO campaign. Turning to Your Honours' fourth question relating to the indictment of the 27th of May, 1999. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber reasonably took into account Sainovic's knowledge of this indictment to infer his JCE intent and this is because this is an additional confirmation that he had the intent. Despite Sainovic's knowledge of the indictment, Sainovic did nothing to encourage the person in charge of the physical perpetrators of a crime listed in the indictment to prosecute or punish them. He did nothing, although he remained in his position as deputy prime minister of the FRY for over a year and a half until the federal government was changed. This is also an additional confirmation that his statements in 1998 and 1999 to the effect that crimes should be punished were "simply window dressing," and in fact Sainovic never intended to deal with the crimes of the FRY and Serbian forces. Turning now to your first question relating to JCE III. Our response to the question is no, Your Honours. If you agree with the Prosecution that the Trial Chamber applied a too-high mens rea standard for JCE III, this will have no impact upon Sainovic's convictions for murder and destruction of and damage to Kosovo Albanian religious property. Indeed, since the Trial Chamber found that these crimes were reasonably foreseeable to Sainovic under a higher probability standard than the required standard, these crimes were clearly foreseeable to Sainovic under the lower, correct, possibility standard. And we rely on our response brief, paragraph 246 to 258 for detailed references to the record. To conclude, Your Honours, all Sainovic's grounds relating to mens rea should be dismissed, and unless Your Honours have any question, this concludes our submissions for today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Your response is really short and straightforward. I'm saying that your response is really short and straightforward. Any reply from defendant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Wait, Judge Pocar has a question. Judge Pocar has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sorry. I agree with the Presiding Judge that your answers were very short, actually, but I wanted to be very clear on one point; it refers to the answer you gave. Is that your position that knowledge of crimes committed in 1998 could be used as a circumstance to show the mens rea for crimes committed in 1999? And that's one point and I believe that's your position clearly. But is your position also the knowledge of crime A committed in 1998 may be sufficient to establish mens rea in 1999 for crime B? Because the question is whether the mens rea for forcible transfer or deportation committed in 1999 could be inferred from crimes other than deportation committed in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. MONCHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: If the knowledge of crimes committed in 1998 other than deportation may be the basis for mens rea for deportation in 1999? Or knowledge of the actual crime, the specific crime, is necessary. We want to be clear about this point as to your position.

utterances.speaker: MS. MONCHY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I think the short response is yes. The reason is because in 1998 the use of excessive and disproportionate force by the FRY and Serbian forces which encompassed a number of crimes; I mean, you had burnings of houses, looting, violence against civilians, including murder, these crimes led to the forcible displacement of the Kosovo Albanian population in 1998. So this is because the accused knows that if these forces would commit the same crime it will further their goal to forcibly displace the Kosovo Albanians in 1999. So that is the reason why other crimes than forcible displacement were relevant to Sainovic's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. I note you said "to possibly displace" in 1999. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MONCHY
utterances.text: Sorry ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, reply from the defendant.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall on behalf of the Sainovic Defence attempt to respond to some of the allegations you've heard today because there is no time for much elaboration. First of all, I would like to make a general comment to what we've heard today from our colleagues from the Prosecution; namely, the response to what our specific grounds of appeal stated in our appeal brief and our arguments today. The response of the Prosecution to all of that is mere reading of certain passages from the trial judgement. The Prosecution explains this approach of theirs by the necessity to interpret the judgement in a holistic way, although even if read in that way each of the findings in the judgement should be subject to further analysis. What we are trying to say that in the judgement there is a whole series of details which taken all together, in combination, lead us to the conclusion that this judgement, as regards Mr. Sainovic, cannot stand. One cannot hide behind the holistic approach and say: This is the judgement, the details should not be analysed. On the contrary, details must be analysed, and if we do that and if you accept our arguments, you come to completely different conclusions than those stated in the trial judgement. Just a few details about what was said by our learned friends from the Prosecution. Speaking of the evidence regarding the existence of the joint criminal enterprise, it is said that there is a pattern of events and that this pattern of events in itself is proof that the JCE exists. My learned friend mentioned today the arming and disarming of the population. I should like to recall that in the trial judgement the Trial Chamber does not dispute the legality, the lawfulness, of arming people. What they do contest is the lawfulness of arming based on ethnic principles. Arming or disarming cannot be viewed in isolation from the events; that is the view of the Defence. At the time when all this is happening between the authorities of the FRY and Serbia on one hand and the authorities of Albanians in Kosovo, there is a conflict, a decade-long conflict. It cannot be expected of lawful authorities in a situation where communications are blocked, roads are blocked, civilians are being killed, there is deep mistrust between the Serb and the Albanian population, it cannot be expected of the authorities of Yugoslavia and Serbia to arm members of a community who are in their majority opposing that army and that police force. In a situation that bears all the characteristics of armed insurgency in Kosovo, it would be unreasonable to conclude or to claim that based on arming or disarming, the conclusion can be made that this is one of the elements built into the joint criminal enterprise. My learned friend also recently mentioned the promotion of Pavkovic and Ojdanic in the context of explaining the role of Mr. Sainovic. I really don't see that anything in the case file could link Mr. Sainovic with the promotions granted to Pavkovic and Ojdanic. Within that pattern of conduct, also mentioned has been the bringing in of additional forces of Yugoslavia and Serbia into Kosovo. That was indicated as one of the proofs of violation of October Agreements and of Serbia's preparation for war. What do we have in the case file? We have evidence that in addition to a certain reinforcement, the increase in numbers of forces present in Kosovo occurs in March 1999; that is to say it is occurring when the NATO air strikes are already a certainty, that things will happen that neither the authorities of Serbia or Yugoslavia want. We also see that NATO is increasing its presence in Macedonia. Their numbers there are 2.000. At the relevant time, in March 1999, the NATO force increases to 12.500. The KLA strength is also much greater. The only logical reaction of the authorities of Yugoslavia and Serbia is to increase their presence and strength in the territory where they are expecting the conflict to occur. That was logically done by the Army of Yugoslavia and the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia and the same would have been done by any other state if it had been in that situation. Let me say a few words about the claim of the Prosecution concerning the pattern of conduct. The Trial Chamber notes also and ascribes responsibility for movements of population exclusively to Serbia. However, the Trial Chamber also notes that there are NATO attacks. It notes the bombing of targets very close to populated areas. It notes that there are reasons that could lead a reasonable trier of fact to make a different conclusion than the one made by the Trial Chamber. However, the Trial Chamber ascribes sole responsibility for the movement of 700.000 people only to the forces of the FRY and Serbia. If there had been any fighting, as there had been around populated areas with the KLA, is that situation important? Should it have been taken into account when deciding when and how these movements of population occurred that the Trial Chamber assesses to have involved at least 700.000 people? If there were other reasons - and the Trial Chamber says there were - each one of them should have been taken into account and weighed properly. So the response in this respect by the Prosecution is inadequate on this issue in the view of this Defence. We have various reports from witnesses and evidence from witnesses as to how these population movements occurred. The Trial Chamber relies solely on the testimony of Albanian witnesses. The evidence that they give is identical. Our learned friend says today that this is because the practice was identical; however, the similarities in witness testimony is simply impossible if evidence is truly given freely and is credible. It is very symptomatic that the greatest number of witnesses come from places where the Kosovo Liberation Army was very, very active and all of these witnesses testified before the Trial Chamber. And down to the last man they denied that in the area from which they fled their homes there had been any serious presence of the KLA or any serious clashes. They simply deny the KLA and the conflict. Even the Trial Chamber finds, with good reason, this irrationality and this inconsistency to indicate that there is something wrong with these witnesses. This should have at least led to some doubt and that doubt would have probably resulted in a different decision by the Trial Chamber. I would also like to refer to the issue of identity papers. The removal of identity papers is also used as proof of pattern of conduct in this case. One should say very briefly on this point that removing identity papers from a person in itself is not very important. Personal details of citizens existed in databases of secretariats of the interior and with other state agencies of Serbia. One's right to citizenship is not lost with the loss of identity papers. The registers of the population which included Serbs and Albanians alike contained all this information. We cannot view this issue in the same way because the loss of identity papers does not lead to loss of citizenship, even if the identity papers were taken away from somebody -- which dominated our discussion today. The Prosecutor even when speaking about the Joint Command quotes passages from the judgement, and it is our impression, with all due respect, that they ignore proper argument. The main thing the Prosecution still ignored today is the huge difference between year 1998 and year 1999. This difference is obvious. This difference is highlighted even by the Trial Chamber. And that is the point, the main thrust, of our appeal. What does the Trial Chamber do and what does the Prosecution support in their arguments today? The Trial Chamber, if it says in its judgement that the Joint Command in 1999 is just evoking prior authority, body of a different nature, all this does not mean that the Joint Command, if it existed in 1998 existed also in 1999 in the same way. We have memories and the reminiscing about prior authority. On a matter so important as the existence or nonexistence of an institution, one cannot make a conclusion based on these things because there is no evidence. What is invoked here today is the order from the Pristina Corps in -- or rather, 16 orders of the Joint Command. And if you here heard the Prosecution today, they also referred to 16 orders of the Pristina Corps with good reason. In the context of these orders, too, it is clear that the chains of command of the army and the MUP are uninterrupted, intact. That is the basis for any proper conclusion as to what exists or not exists in 1999. The 16 orders cannot serve as proof of existence of the Joint Command. Those orders were made in the Pristina Corps. These orders referred to units subordinated to the Pristina Corps, and, quite simply, from their substance we do not see either the necessity or the proof that there is a body, an organ, or an individual who in any way unifies, co-ordinates, harmonises, or influences command functions. Command and the method of co-ordination in 1999 is substantiated even in the trial judgement. The Trial Chamber notes there was a standard practice of the MUP and the Army of Yugoslavia before finalising a plan or an activity involving them jointly; a meeting, a co-ordination meeting is held between the army and the MUP where such co-ordination is ensured. That is normal and that is natural in every situation where two different structures co-operate. In that standard practice there is nowhere either a need or evidence that a third party is needed to arbitrate, especially not a third party who has no knowledge of these matters, a third party who belongs to a political authority or other body. It is clear from the case file why these orders from 1999 have the heading of Joint Command. We have heard testimony from witnesses in this case that this heading designates activities that are jointly carried out with the MUP. There is no mystification here. This is a designation for an order that serves to show that this is a joint action, a joint activity. This is the only explanation. There is no logical or operational need for the involvement of any third party, especially a third party who has nothing to do with police or army co-ordination or has the necessary expertise, as Mr. Sainovic did not. We have heard assertions today, again, that Mr. Sainovic was playing a key part, that his was a central place. But what we haven't heard is the answer. What is the substance of a central place? What does it mean? It is not enough to refer to a central place and then invoke somebody's impressions about that. A central place must have substance. What did Mr. Sainovic do? What did he omit to do? And, most importantly, what in all that had an essential effect on events on the ground, saying that somebody had a central place in itself means nothing. It can be -- it cannot be a basis for any conclusions about Sainovic's position or his role. A good example of this is something that my learned friends mentioned today, a meeting of 16 June. A witness testifies that his impression was that he was respected and listened to. It is quite normal that a deputy prime minister is respected. Wherever he comes in any country in the world, a deputy prime minister would be met with respect. But what if the witness is wrong in his impressions and what is the legal meaning of a witness's impression? Does it have a meaning? We heard what our learned friends had to say, that he interfered in everything, the KVM, the MUP, the Army of Yugoslavia. We heard of a conglomerate of activities, and, with all due respect, that is not discerned even in the trial judgement. Also, trains, train schedules, and so on. However, in the text of the trial judgement we cannot see anything that would be linked to what we heard today. The strong will of Slobodan Milosevic and Nikola Sainovic, agent. What does that mean, strong will of Slobodan Milosevic? When in many places in this judgement there is a clear indication that chains of command are functioning, that Milosevic -- if that is correct and there are many reasons that show that this is not the case but that Milosevic can appoint, dismiss anyone, what does this strong will mean and what does it -- what purpose does it serve? And what about agent Sainovic on the ground? What is the point of that? And this time, the only time that matters after the 24th of March, Milosevic is the supreme commander and he is the man who has the constitutional and legal right to command and control. He does not need a relay. He does not need a mediator. He has the necessary channels, military, police, of course in a specific context, throughout the fact that the police is within one of the federal units. And if we take into account the needs of national defence as such. Also there is the question of co-ordination, co-ordination as my learned friends said, he actually wished to present it as a conspiracy or something verging on conspiracy. Our learned friends for the Prosecution disregard the fact that co-ordination between different structures is something that is a legal and constitutional obligation on the part of different organs of a country and it was also part of police and military practice. A policeman and a soldier do not need a third party to explain the importance of co-ordinator. They know that full well. They know that joint co-ordination can only be materialised through co-ordination. There is nothing mystical about this. There is nothing incredible about this. This is only natural. This is something that anyone who is involved in police work or military work knows full well. Also there is a reference to the question of Milosevic, and now the Defence says that there is no evidence to the effect that anything that existed in 1998 or 1999 on the ground or in communication between Kosovo and Belgrade could have prevented Milosevic from attaining his role as such in 1999. There are no problems in communication. There is clear communication. So he simply does not need Sainovic as an intermediary. All the chains of command, all the chains of communication - this is even established by the Trial Chamber itself - are intact. I would particularly like to note the question of closeness between Sainovic and Milosevic. This is one of the circumstances that has not been fully elucidated. Relations between Sainovic and Milosevic, the content of such a relationship is something that is unknown. There are two or three meetings as a matter of protocol. There is nothing else about any other kind of communication. One can only guess, but guessing or guess-work should not be a basis for any kind of decision. This one meeting or two meetings that might have happened, I mean there's no proof of the content of these meetings and, again, speculation cannot be a basis for saying anything about that. The way in which this relationship is explained would necessitate daily intensive communication, but there is simply no proof of any such thing. Sainovic, the deputy federal prime minister at the time, dismissed from the position of vice-president of the SPS, Sainovic marginalised in many situations that could be of relevance for the Chamber. All of that is in contrast to Milutinovic and that has been sufficiently elaborated upon today. I would also like to refer to the meeting held on the 1st of June, 1999. Again, we heard today that Sainovic was doing something that borders on the incredible. He is conveying the content of an agreement that does not exist. Milosevic-Ahtisaari-Cernomirdin Agreement is an agreement that was concluded only four days later. The negotiations were under way, and, quite simply, something like that is impossible. What is an important question, a very important question, is the question of these channels of communication. The Prosecutor and, unfortunately, the Trial Chamber understand the evidence in this case as follows: Milosevic does not have any other channels of communication and that Sainovic is the only way in which he can reach anyone in Kosovo and the only way in which he can influence events in Kosovo. This really borders on the incredible. Finally, a few moments ago my learned friend raised a question, or rather, tried to provide a response concerning the issuing of the indictment after the things that happened, those that are mentioned in that indictment, that is. And she says that Sainovic could have punished the perpetrators of crimes on that basis. There is no evidence in this case that Sainovic had any kind of authority that would include the punishment of perpetrators of crimes. That is strictly defined in terms of the organs involved, the authority of these organs, in prosecuting the perpetrators of crimes including war crimes and there is no mention of Sainovic in that context. Thank you, Your Honours, I would like to conclude our response in this way to what we heard from the Prosecution today. Thank you.
